10599-lost-in-the-air:
Roy J. Snell published this boys' mystery in 1920, opening with two pals fresh from army aviation service. Bruce Manning, from Canada, and Barney Menter, from the United States, now work developing the wilds of northern Canada near Hudson Bay. Their bookkeeping desks, forest rivers, and cataracts set a romantic, northern stage.

A strange landing, a modern battle with criminals, an infernal machine, a walrus hunt, and a battle beneath the Arctic moon carry the pair toward a treasure city and the pole. A Russian tiger and a mystery cavern add danger. Readers get a fast, old-style air and Arctic adventure for boys.
12461-castles-in-the-air:
Baroness Emmuska Orczy's linked tales are narrated by Hector Ratichon, a French secret agent who served Republic, Empire and King Louis in turn. For twenty years he tracked criminals, nosed out plots and denounced traitors, yet stayed poor, and he tells his cases with pride, grievance and comic self-pity.

One long chapter concerns Theodore, a starving boy Ratichon lifted from a Paris gutter, fed, clothed and made his secretary, only to meet, in his telling, black ingratitude. Other stories turn on spies, disguise and court intrigue. Orczy uses Ratichon's voice to mix adventure with satire, letting a boastful servant of many masters expose the vanity of the regimes he served.
13032-the-book-of-noodles-stories-of-sim:
W. A. Clouston's Book of Noodles, published in 1888, gathers stories of simpletons, fools, and their follies from many lands. Clouston notes that noodle tales, like popular tales generally, seldom trace to a single source, though early Buddhist Jataka birth stories give some an ancient date. Greek jests floated among peoples long before writing fixed them.

A Gaulard tale shows the humour: told the Dean of Besançon is dead, Gaulard disbelieves it, since the dean writes to him about everything and would have told him. Another Gaulard, asked the hour after sunset, cannot tell by the dial. The book delights lovers of folk humour and wise folly.
14468-the-felon-s-track-or-history-of-th:
Michael Doheny, a Young Irelander, wrote this history of the attempted Irish outbreak from 1843 to the close of 1848, issued in Dublin in 1920 with D'Arcy McGee's narrative of 1848 added. Doheny had lived the events he describes.

He traces Daniel O'Connell's movement, the split with Young Ireland, the rising of 1848, and the arrests and exiles that followed, including his own flight. The narrative praises William Smith O'Brien and other leaders amid cheering crowds and hostile halls. The book is partisan history from inside the movement, valuable for its firsthand passion and detail.
14910-elsie-at-the-world-s-fair:
Martha Finley's Elsie at the World's Fair, published by Dodd, Mead in 1894, takes the Elsie family to Chicago's White City. Hugh Lilburn urges his betrothed to a speedy marriage, pleading that her brother has robbed him and his father of their expected housekeeper, his cousin Marian.

Her sisters Isadore and Vi join a party bound for the fair, where exhibits, art and the White City itself become a backdrop for courtship, family talk and moral choice. Finley acknowledges the Chicago Record's history of the fair and fine art series for descriptions and statistics. The novel blends a family story with a guided tour of America's great 1893 show.
15088-proserpina-volume-2-studies-of-way:
John Ruskin's second volume of Proserpina, dated 1888, studies wayside flowers of the Alps, Scotland, and England as his father knew them. He begins with the violet, whose tangled grouping calls for care, and moves through kind after kind with close looks at form, color, and habit. General principles interrupt the special studies from time to time.

Ruskin writes as a teacher and artist, not a dry botanist, and he warns readers not to expect mere pretty praise of violets. His aim is exact seeing: how a flower is built, how it grows, and what its parts do. Nature lovers will find the book patient, opinionated, and full of close observation.
15285-the-hosts-of-the-air:
Joseph Altsheler's 1915 World War novel, The Hosts of the Air, tells a quest in the Great War, with pictures by Charles Wrenn. It belongs to his World War series, beside The Guns of Europe and The Forest of Swords, and follows his Civil War and Young Trailers books. The hero's air quest drives the plot.

Through battles, flights, and escapes, Altsheler blends adventure with wartime romance for young readers. His prose is brisk and patriotic, in the series style. Fans of war adventure will find the novel exciting, if dated in its view of the conflict.
16756-the-bobbsey-twins-at-the-county-fa:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this 1922 Bobbsey Twins tale, issued complete and unabridged by Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Bert, Nan, Flossie, and Freddie head for the county fair after a broken bridge, a snake scare, a merry-go-round, a lost coat, and a crying boy. Fair chapters bring races, a cornfield, a pumpkin, a balloon, an island, and a search party.

Hope keeps the tale gentle and fast, with small frights that end safe and kind helpers at each turn. The twins learn to watch out for each other and for strangers in a crowd. Young readers get a warm, old-style fair adventure, full of rides, races, and family fun, with no real harm in sight.
17821-red-hair:
Elinor Glyn wrote Red Hair in 1905, first run under the title The Vicissitudes of Evangeline, and printed by the Authors' Press at Auburn, New York. The tale is told in diary form by Evangeline, a pretty twenty-year-old with three hundred pounds a year and no home of her own.

Adopted by Mrs. Carruthers in hopes of a fortune, Evangeline is left with nothing when the old lady dies without a fair will. She decides to become an adventuress, living by looks, wit, and charm. Glyn writes with frank, saucy humor about love, money, and the marriage market. It is a lively Edwardian romance, told by a heroine who knows her own mind.
18091-samantha-at-the-world-s-fair:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, wrote Samantha at the World's Fair, printed in New York in 1893 by Funk and Wagnalls, with pictures by Baron C. de Grimm. The book is dedicated to Columbia, who has just sailed out and discovered woman.

Samantha, a Jonesville farm wife, loves Columbus since her old geography days, and she means to see him honored at Chicago. Her preface opens on a fair evening in Jonesville, under a full moon. Holley writes in Samantha's droll, misspelled voice, full of wit and homely wisdom. It is a funny, warm tale of a country woman at the great fair.
18117-georges-guynemer-knight-of-the-air:
Henry Bordeaux wrote Georges Guynemer, Knight of the Air, translated from the French by Louise Morgan Sill, printed in New Haven in 1918 by Yale University Press. The book was published on a fund in memory of Ensign Curtis Seaman Read, killed in France in February 1918, with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt.

Cantos trace Guynemer from childhood, home, and college to his first victory, the Aisne, Verdun, the Somme, and his zenith in May 1917. Bordeaux writes with French pride and a soldier's reverence. It is a moving life of France's great air ace, and a war-time tribute from one hero's memory to another's.
18915-the-poetical-works-of-william-lisl:
The first volume of William Lisle Bowles's poetical works, edited by the Rev. George Gilfillan and published at Edinburgh in 1855, gathers sonnets and miscellaneous poems. Sonnets visit Tynemouth Priory, Bamborough Castle, the Tweed, Dover Cliffs, the Rhine, and Oxford, with elegies, monodies, and songs between.

Longer pieces follow: The Spirit of Discovery, a descriptive and historical poem in five books, and The Missionary in eight cantos. A ninth edition of the poems had been called for, and the memoir and critical dissertation, delayed, were promised for the second volume. The book shows a clergyman-poet of the old school, at home in landscape, memory, and devotion.
20421-proserpina-volume-1-studies-of-way:
Proserpina is John Ruskin's study of wayside flowers, written for readers who want to look at plants with care. This first volume grew from Ruskin's own early study of botany. He recalls the first botany book he used, Curtis's Magazine, published in 1795.

Ruskin praises that old magazine's plates as excellent and says he is always glad to find them. His own pages mix close looking at leaves and petals with thoughts on art and naming. The book teaches botany as an act of attention: see the flower rightly, and knowledge follows.
2172-that-mainwaring-affair:
Hugh Mainwaring sits at the head of a business firm, a man near fifty whose neat desk and polished manners mark him as a shrewd financier. Maynard Barbour sets this novel in the world of offices, money, and family standing, where a respected name can hide a tangle of private dealings. The story turns on what lies behind the firm's orderly surface.

As the affair unfolds, questions about loyalty, money, and reputation press on Mainwaring and those around him. Barbour keeps the focus on character and motive rather than on action alone. Readers who like a slow, careful mystery of business life will find a portrait of a man whose public success and private troubles pull in opposite ways.
21819-kalli-the-esquimaux-christian-a-me:
Kallihirua, called Kalli, was an Inuk from the far Arctic whose short life is told in this sixpenny memoir by the Reverend T. B. Murray. The book was issued by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Kalli was plain and short, the text admits, and looked what he was. Yet all who knew his story and his docile mind felt interest and regard for him.

Brought from his Greenland home into contact with British sailors and teachers, Kalli learned English ways and the Christian faith. Murray, who also wrote on Pitcairn Island, tells the tale for church readers at home. It is a small book with a wide reach: the Arctic, the navy, and the mission field meet in one young life.
21919-teachers-outlines-for-studies-in-e:
High school English teachers get a full set of lesson plans in Gilbert Sykes Blakely's Teachers' Outlines for Studies in English, published in 1908. Blakely taught English at Morris High School in New York City. His outlines follow the college admission requirements of the day, book by book. The novel comes first: he notes that nearly every reading boy and girl loves novels, which gives the teacher a fine opening.

Outlines cover Ivanhoe, Silas Marner, and Cranford, and poems like The Ancient Mariner. Five plays of Shakespeare, plus Comus, and essays from Franklin to Macaulay follow. Each outline points the teaching at the text's heart. The book is a window on the classic school canon of 1908, and on how it was taught.
23167-the-man-in-the-reservoir:
Charles Fenno Hoffman climbs down into trouble in The Man in the Reservoir. Weeds grow from a half-dozen cracks in the masonry, the narrator points out. In one such crack he set his foot and started down the wall. The reservoir then stood fuller than today, its water only a few strides below him.

New York's Croton Reservoir, a city wonder of Hoffman's day, becomes the stage for a rescue remembered in exact, toehold detail. Hoffman, poet and editor, writes the descent as if his reader's foot were on the stone. The tale belongs to the early American magazine tradition, fact and thrill in equal parts. Its masonry still holds.
234-child-christopher-and-goldilind-the-:
William Morris sets a medieval romance in Oakenrealm, a woodland where a squirrel could cross tree to tree. Child Christopher and Goldilind the Fair, published in 1895, opens with a warrior king who wins a bride and lays down his armor for love. Their son Christopher inherits the realm's troubles.

Morris writes in archaic, musical prose full of forests, courts, and quests. Christopher and Goldilind face separation, tyranny, and wandering before reunion. The tale revives chivalric romance for Victorian readers. It shows Morris the craftsman as storyteller. Morris's romance influenced fantasy writers who prized invented worlds and old speech.
23999-a-day-at-the-county-fair:
Alice Hale Burnett published A Day at the County Fair in New York in 1916, a Merryvale Girls story with pictures by Charles F. Lester. Burnett also wrote Beth's Garden Party and Geraldine's Birthday Surprise, and the fair book follows her young heroines for a single crowded day.

It opens with Jerry, Geraldine White, begging Mary Lee for a harder swing, so she can fly up to the tree tops. Beth Burton comes flying down the street, and the invitation follows. Chapters bring a motor trip, a picnic lunch, the greased pole, Jerry's treat, and Uncle Billy's story. An exciting moment, with a huge ball rising slowly in the air, sends the girls home again.
24562-the-panjab-north-west-frontier-pro:
Sir James Douie wrote this history and description of the Panjab, the North-West Frontier Province, and Kashmir. The Seema Publications edition, printed at Delhi in 1974, reprints a classic provincial history, with maps and illustrations. Its chapters cover the land, its peoples, and its rulers.

Douie, a former administrator, writes with the knowledge of a man who governed the region. His book moves from early history through Sikh rule and British administration to the frontier tribes and Kashmir. Readers who want a solid, old-fashioned guide to north-west India will find it full of detail and judgement.
24666-the-voyages-of-the-ranger-and-crus:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this sea tale of two ships, the Ranger and the Crusader. The Ranger serves the navy mainly carrying troops to India and other places where Britain strove to keep the peace. The Crusader serves as an emigrant ship, carrying people seeking a new life in New Zealand.

Kingston notes that some emigrants were a useless lot, whom no life anywhere would suit, but his book also shows the pluck and courage of better emigrants under adversity. Both ships meet trouble, and the story follows passengers and crews through storm, hardship, and rescue. Young readers get a stirring double voyage tale.
24813-the-queen-s-scarlet-the-adventures:
George Manville Fenn wrote The Queen's Scarlet about Dick Frayne, a seventeen-year-old baronet studying for the Army exam. After a fight with his cousin Mark, Dick is thought drowned: a shepherd boy's body is buried in his place, and Mark takes the estate. Dick instead enlists as a bandsman, flute in hand, and serves in a garrison town.

Fate brings Mark to the same town as an officer, and a shooting in a hop field leaves Dick for dead until hop workers find him alive. Nursed back to health, Dick wins back his title and lands, passes his exam, and takes a commission. Fenn tells a brisk tale of mistaken death, family wrong, and a young man earning his scarlet coat.
25206-rollo-s-philosophy-air:
Jacob Abbott's Rollo's Philosophy: Air, one of fourteen Rollo volumes, teaches children about the air through talk and experiment. A revised edition from Phillips, Sampson of Boston presents the discussions as lessons in thinking, reasoning, and observation rather than mere facts.

Rollo and his father work through experiments with cylinders and pistons, learning that air springs back when pressure is removed. The property is called elasticity, or the expansive force of air. Abbott keeps the language simple, so young readers grasp both the science and the habit of careful thought.
25579-ralph-the-heir:
Anthony Trollope's novel Ralph the Heir first ran in Saint Paul's Magazine in 1870 and 1871, then appeared in book form in 1871 with pictures by F. A. Fraser. A scene on the lawn at Popham Villa, with sherry, soda water, and a pipe, fronts the story's easy country-house world.

Chapters introduce Sir Thomas, Popham Villa, Mary Bonner, Mr. Neefit and his family, Ralph Newton's troubles, and Ontario Moggs, before turning to Newton Priory. Trollope weighs inheritance, marriage, money, and duty through two Ralphs and the families around them, in his usual clear, talkative prose.
26018-granny-s-wonderful-chair:
Frances Browne tells fairy tales round a wonderful chair in Granny's Wonderful Chair, from Blackie's Stories Old and New series for children. The series preface likens a small chosen library to a walled garden where a child may safely play. It promises real books, well printed and bound, with old tales that never grow old beside new ones. Contents run from an introduction and the Christmas cuckoo to Lady Greensleeves, Childe Charity, and Prince Wisewit's return.

Lady Greensleeves chats with a great black raven in the forest, asking news of his part of the woods. The raven says in a hundred years they will be genteel and private, trees grown so thick. He tells of a fairy king who spelled two lords for thinning his oaks for poor men's firewood. The tales mix wonder, kindness, and old magic in plain, child sized prose.
26044-peter-and-jane-or-the-missing-heir:
S. Macnaughtan tells a comedy of manners and a missing heir in Peter and Jane, first printed in 1911 and reprinted through a sixth edition in 1919. Mrs. Ogilvie, her red hair in the currently fashionable shade and her gown by Paquin, sits reading the Court Journal. She thinks on Aristotelian lines, scorns most women save Charlotte Corday, Judith, and Joan of Arc, and dyes her hair, a fact strangers mistake for a wig.

Later scenes show Mrs. Avory, worn and thin, eyes large in a sallow face, after late nights at work and household bothers that weigh on her heart. A friend orders a motor car to meet her at the station, planning tea in the library and every comforting word he can find. Macnaughtan writes of smart folk, thin purses, and kind hearts with wit.
26335-brite-and-fair:
Henry A. Shute's Brite and Fair, issued by the Cosmopolitan Book Corporation in 1920 with pictures by Worth Brehm, is a boy's diary from the 1860s, written in the boy's own rough spelling. Entries open on a June Sunday, when the family leaves the Unitarian church for the Congregational, since Keene and Cele sing in the choir. Beany, the organ blower, peeks out, pulls faces, and gets yanked from the loft by the superintendent.

Later entries bring a new minister preaching against killing flies, bugs, and hornets, and washing day lugging pails for old Miss Dire. The diarist rises early to tend Nellie, sweep the stable, and black his father's boots before a Boston trip. The book gives 1860s town boyhood in a voice full of mischief and chores.
26732-free-air:
Sinclair Lewis, author of The Job, published this road novel with Grosset and Dunlap at New York, copyrighted in 1919 by Harcourt, Brace and Howe. Its first chapter is Miss Boltwood of Brooklyn Is Lost in the Mud. Claire Boltwood, driving a seventy-horsepower Gomez-Dep roadster, finds Minnesota country roads have no respect for her polite Long Island parkway experience.

Rain films the windshield until Claire fancies she pilots a drowned car under the sea, then drops jab into her eyes when it opens. A patch of gravel promises speed, then ends in wet black ruts and prairie gumbo, a sticky mire the book compares to tar, fly-paper, fish glue, and chewed sweets. Claire escapes from respectability, meets a young man in a raincoat, and travels through sagebrush tourists, adventurers by firelight, and the fallacy of romance toward the free woman.
27015-more-science-from-an-easy-chair:
Sir Ray Lankester's More Science from an Easy Chair gathers popular science essays by a working naturalist writing for general readers. The chapters wander from a day in the Oberland and Switzerland in early summer to Gletsch and the problem of the galloping horse.

Other essays take up the jewel in the toad's head, elephants, a strange extinct beast, and vegetarians and their teeth, with food, cookery, smells, and perfumes alongside. Lankester explains with clarity and wit, making hard natural history feel like talk from a well-stocked armchair. The volume carries 34 illustrations, and Lankester held honours including the K.C.B. and fellowship of the Royal Society.
27147-the-stretton-street-affair:
William Le Queux's The Stretton Street Affair, published by Macaulay in 1922, opens with a cry over a dead niece: Gabrielle, my poor niece, she's dead. The prologue introduces Oswald de Gex, and the chapters follow the sister's story and the question of who Gabrielle Engledue was.

Later chapters bring the city of the lily, the millionaire's apprehensions, Monsieur Suzor again, and cries of red, green and gold, toward the gate of the sun. Le Queux spins a postwar mystery of wealth, secrets, and pursuit across London and Italy. The book was printed in the United States by the Macaulay Company. Chapters include Little Mrs. Cullerton and Some Plain Speaking.
27157-historic-boys-their-endeavours-the:
E. S. Brooks's Historic Boys, published in 1886 with illustrations by R. B. Birch and John Schönberg, selects a dozen young fellows of different lands and epochs. The preface argues that manliness and self-reliance have ever been the groundwork of character, from the second century to the nineteenth.

The frontispiece shows Marcus Annius Verus, afterward the emperor Marcus Aurelius, from a bust in the Capitoline Museum. Each life shows a boy who, even before manhood, left an impress on his time by braving danger, difficulty, or death for good or evil.
27277-little-brothers-of-the-air:
Olive Thorne Miller's Little Brothers of the Air, published by Houghton, Mifflin in 1893, gathers bird studies written on Long Island's Great South Bay and in New York's Black River Country. Some chapters first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's Bazaar, and the Independent.

The contents run from the kingbird's nest and a chronicle of three little kings to the veery mother, the tawny thrush's brood, a bobolink rhapsody, and the wiles of a warbler. Miller names birds by the American Ornithological Society's list, watching nests, songs, and mothers with patient affection.
28642-joe-strong-on-the-trapeze-or-the-d:
Vance Barnum's Joe Strong on the Trapeze, published by the Whitman Publishing Company of Racine with copyright 1916, continues the Joe Strong series. Earlier volumes made Joe a boy wizard, a boy fish, and a high-wire performer, with wings of steel and a box of mystery still to come. This volume promises the daring feats of a young circus performer.

The tale opens in a theatre, where Joe and Professor Alonzo Rosello bow to applause for black art, magic, illusion, and legerdemain. A pigeon-omelet trick gives way to the fire trick, its apparatus overhauled and its electric current trusted. Joe's vanishing trick, chair, black cloth, and unbroken newspaper sheet, was explained in the Boy Wizard volume. Chapters carry Joe off to the circus and through Helen's inheritance.
29069-poisoned-air:
Captain S. P. Meek published this story in Astounding Stories in March 1932, bringing back his hero Dr. Bird for another clash with the villain Saranoff. The action opens at the Aberdeen Proving Ground, where a hospital orderly takes a call from a man racked by violent coughing fits, unable to get more than a few words out.

A deadly, mysterious blanket of fog hangs over the ground, and Bird must trace its source and stop Saranoff before more men fall to it. Meek pairs laboratory detective work with pulp menace: a weapon in the air itself. Readers get a tense early science fiction thriller about poison gas, a hidden enemy, and a scientist racing a spreading danger.
29718-the-automobile-storage-battery-its:
O. A. Witte, chief engineer of the American Bureau of Engineering, wrote The Automobile Storage Battery: Its Care and Repair, third edition completely revised and enlarged, fourth impression, published in 1922. The book explains, in plain language, the theory, build, working, making, upkeep, and fixing of the lead-acid battery used on cars. Sections on radio and farm lighting batteries stand beside it.

Witte describes the simple battery, or voltaic cell, chemical actions that make a cell produce electricity, and the difference between primary and storage cells. The book aims to help a repairman build a successful battery business. Readers of automotive history will find a thorough, practical manual from the age of the early motor car.
29732-the-old-arm-chair:
Eliza Cook's Old Arm-Chair, printed in Boston in 1886 by D. Lothrop and Company with pictures by Miss L. B. Humphrey and others, opens with a cry of love for an old chair. The speaker has cherished it as a sainted prize, wept over it, and embalmed it with sighs, bound by a thousand bands to the heart.

The spell is a mother who sat there, nursing her child and dying in that seat. In childhood's hour the speaker lingered near, hearing gentle words to fit one to die and teach one to live. Readers of Victorian verse will find a tender, famous poem of home, memory, and a mother's chair.
29734-experiments-and-observations-on-di:
Joseph Priestley, LL.D., F.R.S., wrote these Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air, priced at five shillings unbound, after the favorable reception of his earlier observations on air. The book's Latin epigraph prays that men, setting aside flighty philosophies, return with humility to the volume of creation and linger over God's works. Priestley's experiments isolate, weigh, and name the airs that fill our world.

The work stands among the founding texts of pneumatic chemistry, leading toward oxygen and the new chemistry. Priestley writes as experimenter and philosopher at once. Students of science history will find a landmark book where careful experiment first mapped the airs we breathe.
29879-the-poetical-works-of-william-coll:
Little, Brown and Company printed this Boston edition of William Collins's poems in 1865. A memoir by Sir Harris Nicolas opens the volume, followed by an essay on the genius and poems of Collins by Sir Egerton Brydges. The poems themselves begin with the Oriental Eclogues: Selim the shepherd, Hassan the camel driver, Abra the Georgian sultana, and Agib and Secander the fugitives.

The odes follow in full: To Pity, To Fear, To Simplicity, To Liberty, To Evening, and To Peace among them. The Passions, the ode on the death of Thomson, and the ode on Highland superstitions show Collins at his best. Dr. Langhorne's observations on the eclogues and the odes close the book. It is a handsome, scholarly edition of a short-lived poet.
30087-amaryllis-at-the-fair:
Richard Jefferies wrote Amaryllis at the Fair, reissued in London in 1904 by Duckworth and Company and reprinted in the Readers' Library in 1911. Jefferies had already written The Gamekeeper at Home, After London, Wood Magic, and Bevis. He dedicates the book to Charles Prestwich Scott. An Alcaeus epigraph fronts it: our day is but a finger, bring large cups. The Readers' Library lists it among uniform volumes by Belloc, Birrell, Bourne, Galsworthy, and others.

The introduction opens on a phrase often in critics' mouths: the book is not a novel. Jefferies takes up that common critical formula at the start, in a volume that resists easy sorting into novel or essay. Readers coming to Jefferies for his nature writing and rural observation will find the same hand here, turned to a fair-day world.
30584-the-covent-garden-theatre-or-pasqu:
Pasquin Turned Drawcansir, subtitled The Covent Garden Theatre, survives in a text prepared from a handwritten copy, probably by a professional copyist, with line endings regularized by added dashes of variable length. Some real dashes are therefore conjectural, and typographic variants appear as underlining or smaller writing.

Abbreviations such as Mister appear in simplified form from superscript originals, and an HTML version offers illustrative images of portions of the text. The play satirizes Covent Garden theater, its managers, and its audiences through the Pasquin tradition of mockery. It serves theater historians and readers of eighteenth-century stage satire in a carefully transcribed form. The tone is sly and brisk. It pokes fun at stage folk, their pride, and their crowds, with jokes that still land today.
30697-alaska-days-with-john-muir:
S. Hall Young wrote this 1915 memoir of days spent with John Muir in Alaska, with pictures of glaciers, lakes, and Muir himself. Young, a minister and traveler, recalls Muir among spruce cones, on boats, and on ice. The book's seven chapters run from The Mountain and The Rescue through The Voyage, The Discovery, and The Lost Glacier. A map of their voyages sits inside.

The book mixes adventure with close looks at wild country: bergs sailing out of a bay, a glacier sleeping between granite walls, and crevasses on the ice. Young shows Muir as a keen walker, talker, and watcher, full of joy in rough places. Readers who love Muir, Alaska, or early travel writing will find a warm, first-hand portrait of a naturalist at work.
31361-the-deaves-affair:
Hulbert Footner's 1922 mystery, published by A. L. Burt in New York, opens in an attic studio over Washington Square. There the painter Evan Weir, finding everything out of kilter, cuts up a still life of a broken jar, three books, and Persian embroidery and burns it in the empty stove. Twenty-four chapters and a postscript follow a penny change, a rich man's house, snooping, a new lodger, a happy little family, and the little fellow in grey.

Later chapters bring platonic friendship, Evan re-engaged, a smashed compact, Maud's interest, the steamboat Ernestina, and detective work. They go on to Number 11 Van Dorn Street, the club house, an accident, four visits from George Deaves, and Simeon Deaves turning philanthropist. Lively and urbane, the novel is a classic American mystery of manners and detection.
31670-a-discourse-for-the-time-delivered:
W. H. Furness, pastor of the First Congregational Unitarian Church, delivered this discourse for the time on January 4, 1852, and it was printed at Philadelphia by C. Sherman in 1852. Furness takes his text from Romans 14:7, "None of us liveth to himself," and he speaks from it to the condition of the country in his own day.

He begins by referring to facts that mark a brutal and ruthless military temper, and he presses the truth that no life stands alone. The sermon argues that private conduct and public duty are bound together, and that a congregation must weigh its own part in the wrongs of the time.
32303-pastoral-affair:
Charles A. Stearns's science-fiction tale, printed in Galaxy in February 1959, opens with Colonel Glinka landing by seaplane on a lonely sandspit off the Arabian Sea. He steps ashore in khaki shorts and a pith helmet, watched in silence by burnoosed figures on the arid ridges above the jetty. The place looks barren and unwelcoming, far from any picture of a tropical paradise.

Glinka's mission soon collides with Stefanik, a local man determined to fight rather than hand his children over to the colonel. The story plays that clash for both humour and tension, as military bluster meets stubborn family loyalty on a remote shore. Its title points to the pastoral setting where a small, personal dispute carries larger stakes.
33073-the-arm-chair:
The Arm Chair, in a second edition printed at Philadelphia in 1843, is a poem about a chair and the worthies who sat in it. Its memorandum explains that an arm chair made many years earlier by John Letchworth for Leonard and Jane Snowdon was presented to the author. It adds news of the guests who visited its estimable owners, and a hint that it would suit some verses. The poem that follows takes Cowper, poet of the Christian muse who sang of the sofa, as its model.

The verses praise Letchworth, now fourscore years and four, honest as sunshine, who scooped the seat, trimmed elbows and uprights, and made feet with an artist's skill. From that chair the poem looks back on visitors, talk, and a household's history. It is a gentle, old-fashioned piece, fond of furniture as memory, and it preserves a small domestic world in rhyme.
33405-familiar-talks-on-science-world-bu:
Elisha Gray's Familiar Talks on Science, volume one, World-Building and Life: Earth, Air, and Water, copyrighted in 1899, explains nature in plain, friendly talks. Gray, a noted inventor, opens with world-building and life, then moves through limestone, coal, slate and shale, and salt, before turning to air and water. His aim is to make science clear to readers without a lab.

The book's charm lies in its talk-like style, where each chapter takes one common thing and shows the forces behind it. Gray writes for families and schools, with wonder rather than jargon. For readers who enjoy old popular science, it is a pleasant, instructive volume, full of the earth sciences as the nineteenth century knew them.
33664-norine-s-revenge-and-sir-noel-s-he:
May Agnes Fleming pairs two popular novels in this volume: Norine's Revenge and Sir Noel's Heir. Fleming, whose many novels included Guy Earlscourt's Wife, A Wonderful Woman, and A Terrible Secret, was praised by her publishers for life-like conversation and flashes of wit. They also praised her constantly varying scenes and deeply interesting plots. The two titles promise the sensation fiction her readers expected: a woman's revenge and a disputed inheritance.

Bound together at a dollar and a half, the novels offer Victorian melodrama of love, wrong, and retribution, with heroines who fight back against the men and circumstances that wronged them. Readers who enjoy nineteenth-century popular romance with strong incident and emotional stakes will find Fleming's storytelling swift, vivid, and unabashedly theatrical.
33723-phiz-hablot-knight-browne-a-memoir:
Fred G. Kitton memorializes Hablot Knight Browne, known as Phiz, in this 1882 memoir, with a portrait and numerous illustrations, including a selection from Browne's correspondence and notes on his principal works. A Punch obituary verse opens the book. The lamp is out that lighted the text of Dickens and Lever, and readers who love Pickwick and Lorrequer place next the man who made them see such men. Martin Chuzzlewit, Mr. Dombey, Uriah Heep, and Peggotty all live through his drawings.

Kitton traces Browne's career from his birth in 1815 to his death in July 1882, showing how an illustrator could become a hero of the pen in his own right. The memoir argues that there is no death for such a man, since he lives on in picture books with the characters he drew. It remains a warm, essential source on Victorian illustration.
34098-science-of-trapping-describes-the-:
E. Kreps wrote this revised manual on the science of trapping, published at Saint Louis in 1909 by A. R. Harding. Kreps describes fur-bearing animals, their nature, habits, and distribution, with practical methods for their capture. Chapters run from the trapper's art through skunk, mink, weasel, marten, fisher, otter, and beaver.

Muskrat, fox, wolf, bear, raccoon, badger, opossum, lynx, cougar, wolverine, pocket gopher, and rabbit follow, with tracks and signs, handling furs, and steel traps to close. Pictures show sets in place and catches. The book remains a thorough guide to the trapper's trade.
34996-the-delafield-affair:
Florence Finch Kelly, who wrote With Hoops of Steel, set this novel in the West she knew well. McClurg of Chicago printed The Delafield Affair on March 6, 1909. Four plates in colour by Maynard Dixon, a famed hand at western scenes, grace the book.

Vengeance Avowed opens the tale, and The Evil That Men Do follows hard. Mistake or Blunder, The Powers Confer, and a stiff chapter of rebuke fill the early list. A plate at the front shows a man smiling down at a glowing young face, his eyes bright with praise. Love and a feud over land or name seem set to clash, in the western manner Kelly's readers prized.
35132-the-promise-of-air:
Algernon Blackwood, who wrote The Centaur and A Prisoner in Fairyland, stands behind this novel of a man's strange growth. Macmillan printed The Promise of Air in London in 1918. Joseph Wimble, its hero, starts life in a plain, rich home.

Joseph is the only son of a chemist who made a fortune from an invisible sticking plaster. Charterhouse and Cambridge train the boy to be a gentleman. His father quits trade, calls himself an Expert, and plans a grand tour of Europe as a cap. To talk with ease of Rome, Vienna, and Constantinople helps a man with women, he says. Blackwood takes that smooth start and bends it toward his known theme: the unseen world.
35884-john-patrick-third-marquess-of-but:
John Patrick, Third Marquess of Bute is a memoir by David Hunter Blair, printed by John Murray at London in 1921. A frontispiece shows the Marquess at nine with his mother, from a picture at Mount Stuart. Blair was the Marquess's friend, and writes to his memory. The contents divide the life by its seasons.

Early life runs from 1847 to 1861. Harrow and Christ Church follow, to 1866. Religious inquiries, a postponed reception, and a coming of age fill 1867 and 1868. At Danesfield comes the reception into the Catholic Church. The Western Mail, Rome and the Council, and a return to Scotland cover 1869 to 1871. Marriage, home and family life, and a visit to Majorca follow. Two chapters treat his literary work on the Scottish Review. The memoir is of a great Welsh landowner who was also a scholar, a convert, and a builder.
363-the-oakdale-affair:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sets this short mystery in a small town where a bank president's house stands dark above the lawn. A young thief slips in by night, takes a chauffeur's clothes, and finds far more trouble than loot. What starts as a burglary soon tangles with a missing girl, a murder charge, and a town quick to judge.

The youth, whose grace and nerve hint at a past far above crime, must clear his name while the law closes in. Burroughs plays the tale as both puzzle and chase, with clues, disguises, and a sharp twist at the end. The book moves fast and leans on suspense more than on long talk.
36858-the-blockade-of-phalsburg-an-episo:
The Blockade of Phalsburg is a tale of the end of the Empire, turned into English from the French of Erckmann-Chatrian. It forms part of a set of tales of French history in story form. The book came out in New York from Charles Scribner's Sons in an edition with pictures. A note at the front picks out one figure for praise.

That figure is the Jew Moses, who tells the tale. The note calls his portrait one of the most glad in the whole gallery of the two authors. The list of pictures gives a taste of the scenes: a frontispiece of a field of the dead, a call on a sergeant, and a sortie from a tile-kiln. The tale is cast as a first-hand account of a siege in the last days of Napoleon's rule.
36975-the-lost-heir:
Henty wrote this adventure novel, The Lost Heir, printed by the Mershon Company of Rahway and New York. Henty had written Sturdy and Strong and Rujub the Juggler before it. Twenty-six chapters carry the plot, and a picture shows Simcoe rushing in with his knife against a tiger. The tale opens in India, near the bungalow of Brigadier-General Mathieson at Benares.

Soldiers say the general has been badly hurt and is borne down in litters, with relays of bearers each five miles. Chapter heads add the South Seas, a deaf girl, a gypsy, and a gambling den. John Simcoe and his friend take up the middle of the book. A startling will, an advertisement, and a fresh clew drive the search for the heir.
37006-fire-cloud-or-the-mysterious-cave-:
Fire Cloud, or the Mysterious Cave, is a tale of Indians and pirates by Samuel Fletcher. The book stands in a frontier set of cheap tales for the post trade. Rights date the work to the year nineteen nine. Its first lines own that the tale came by word of mouth through kin.

Old Ben told the tale to an uncle, who held it true in each part. Cave scenes lay at a hill foot where great rocks roll down with time. Those falls may have shut the cave mouth for good in late years, it says. Fire Cloud, the chief of the title, lends the tale its wild core. Sea rogues and red men clash in the stock dime book mode.
3729-widger-s-quotations-from-project-gu:
David Widger compiled this quote book from the memoirs of Napoleon, gathering short passages that can be read in any order. The lines come from the recollections of those who knew the emperor at close range, and they range from court gossip at Malmaison to notes on temper, vanity, and power. A lovesick gentleman haunting Hortense's carriage with flowers, hair, and verses shows the human scale of the collection.

The book serves browsers rather than scholars, since each entry stands alone and needs no context to amuse or sting. Readers hunting for a sharp line on Napoleon, his family, or his court will find plenty here. It also works as a sampler, pointing back to the full memoirs for those who want the long story behind a single vivid sentence.
37362-beautiful-bulbous-plants-for-the-o:
Beautiful Bulbous Plants for the Open Air is a gardening book by John Weathers of Kew. It belongs to his Beautiful series, beside volumes on roses, flowering trees and garden flowers.

Weathers argues in his preface that bulbous plants had not received the attention they deserve in gardening literature, for all the articles in the papers. Lilies and narcissi had their great monographs, by Elwes, Burbidge and Baker, and the crocus had Herbert and Maw. But the class as a whole wanted a book. His plates, beginning with ixias, show the range of colour these plants offer the open garden. The volume is Edwardian practical horticulture: a specialist's survey made handsome for the amateur's shelf.
37647-the-adventures-of-a-country-boy-at:
The Adventures of a Country Boy at a Country Fair, by James Otis, was published at Boston in 1893. Otis had written Toby Tyler. Thirty two chapters carry the tale. Chapter one is called A Young Fakir. Teddy Hargreaves begs leave to run a cane and knife board at the Peach Bottom fair. Deacon Jones will rent him the right for ten dollars. Uncle Nathan will lend the stock money. Teddy hopes to earn enough to pay his mother's debt on the place.

His aunt calls the plan mad as a March hare. His father worked a whole life and never got three or four hundred dollars together, she says. Later heads promise fakirs, burglars, arrests, and a trial. Sam cries stop thief in the front plate.
38060-out-of-the-air:
Inez Haynes Irwin's Out of the Air was published in New York by Grosset & Dunlap, under copyrights of 1920 and 1921. Irwin gives the book to Billy and Phyllis. The story opens inside a letter, typed out in a Washington Square apartment on an early June day.

David Lindsay is writing to Spink Sparrel, and his first answer is flat: no, he does not want ever to fly again. His last pay-hop was two Saturdays ago, his discharge papers came yesterday, and, God willing, he will never ride anything more dangerous than a velocipede again. The letter runs on to praise the apartment Sparrel found him, the key house of New York, with its sailor's chest, butterfly table, and glass lamps. Twice, though, Lindsay breaks off, staring at the doorway as if jerked out of himself.
40212-a-letter-to-the-society-for-the-su:
Richard Carlile wrote a public letter to the Society for the Suppression of Vice, printed in London in 1819. Associated persecutors, he begins, your envenomed and malign spirit precludes any apology for addressing you. They had immured him within the walls of a prison, he says, and fancy a demoniac smile at having crushed him.

Be not too sanguine, he warns. Neither fear of imprisonment nor fear of death shall deter him from propagating his principles of true morality. What is the religion you profess, he asks, that alarms at every attempt to investigate its merits. Why fear to be left naked as the breeze leaves the stem of the woolly dandelion. Carlile's defiance is a classic of free enquiry under prosecution.
41922-the-bedroom-and-boudoir:
The Bed-Room and Boudoir is a guide to the dress of sleep rooms by Lady Barker, put out at London in the late eighteen seventies. It had reached its fifth run of print by the date of the copy at hand. A short word first, by a named hand, frames its aim in plain terms.

Too much care can not be spent on our sleep rooms, that word says, if we would have them sound, handy, and bright. The worth of good sleep to busy folk, most of all to those who work with the brain, can not be set too high. Its parts then take an ideal room in turn: walls, floor cloths and drapes, beds and their dress, clothes stores, and fire and light.
42015-helen-in-the-editor-s-chair:
Helen in the Editor Chair is a girls novel by Ruthe Wheeler, copyrighted in 1932. Its heroine Helen Blair is a schoolgirl tied to a small town weekly paper. Chapter one, The Weekly Herald, opens on press day with Helen watching the school clock. Five slow minutes stand between her and the dismissal bell she longs for.

Contents promise startling news, a storm, reporting plus, and the first issue under her hand. Mystery in the night and a rescue on Lake Dubar raise the stakes mid book. Behind the footlights and a special assignment test the young editor in turn. An exclusive story and success close her run in the editor chair.
46117-the-dreadnought-of-the-air:
Percy Westerman wrote The Dreadnought of the Air, for Partridge at London. It stands in a glories of sea and air series. A front plate shows an airship looping with her motors still running. Contents open with Sub-Lieutenant Dacres and a French instructor. Removed from the navy list and a mysterious airship follow.

A momentous train journey, a challenge, and the airship's return come next. The flight to London and the stolen plans fill the middle. An airship called the Meteor makes her debut. Across Greenland and to the North Pole the tale then flies. In the nick of time, a bold stroke, and a disaster follow. Within a prison, a brush with Indians, and a president's visit close in. It opens on make and mend clothes day in the navy. Westerman gives boys sea and sky at full stretch.
46258-thorley-weir:
Thorley Weir is a novel by E F Benson, published by J B Lippincott of Philadelphia and London in 1913. Benson had earlier written The Image in the Sand and Paul. The book runs in ten plain numbered chapters. A weir on a river gives the novel its name and its setting.

The opening paints a famous Benson heat wave. The hottest day of the hottest June begins to abate toward evening. For six weeks an unveiled sun has baked the pavements of the close packed cities. Providence, Benson jokes, resented complaints that hot summers were past. The joke stopped amusing long ago, he admits. From that sweltering start the story moves to the river world of the weir. Benson's light social comedy plays out among people escaping the town heat.
46287-the-book-of-vagabonds-and-beggars-:
Hotten Englished this book of vagabonds and beggars with their word list. Hotten printed it at Piccadilly, London, in the year 1860. Martin Luther edited the work first in the year 1528. Hotten gives an introduction and notes to the old German text.

The preface calls it a picture of vagabond ways before the Reformation. In England the Liber Vagatorum was near unknown, he writes there. Luther preface and editorship give the small book its weight. Hotten kept the antique style to hold its quaint old spirit. A facsimile woodcut of the old print stands among the front matter of the edition.
47169-buenos-ayres-and-the-provinces-of-:
Sir Woodbine Parish's Buenos Ayres and the Provinces of the Rio de la Plata was published by John Murray of London in 1839. Parish had served many years as His Majesty's charge d'affaires at Buenos Ayres, and most of his matter was gathered in that post. The full title promises the present state, trade, and debt of the provinces.

It also promises, from original documents, an account of geographical discovery in South America across the last sixty years. The introduction tells how Spain hid that knowledge away: her settlements on the Patagonian coast and her surveys of the Pampas stayed locked in secret archives. Fear that Britain, fresh from the Falkland Islands, might forestall her drove the exploring.
4754-the-philosophy-of-despair:
David Starr Jordan dedicates this book to John Maxson Stillman. It opens The Philosophy of Despair with a verse on a darkening sky, a whitening sea, and wind in tall palm trees. Soon or late, the verse says, comes a call from mountain or sea. A friend may write on grey sea wall that the speaker loved God's earth, and earth loved him. Jordan then states his theme plainly.

Today is your day and mine, he says. It is the only day we have, in which we play our part. Its meaning in the great whole we may not grasp, but we are here to act, not to whine, and to express love in human helpfulness. Any other course, learned from sad experience, leads toward decay and waste. Readers get a short, hopeful essay against despair, with Jordan's opening on the bubbles of Saki, urging action over cynicism.
47923-runnymede-and-lincoln-fair:
Runnymede and Lincoln Fair, a story of the Great Charter by Edgar, appears here in Everyman's Library, first issued in 1908 and reprinted in 1914. Dent printed it in London and Dutton in New York, with an introduction by Hughes. Edgar's earlier books for boys, listed at the front, run from Biography for Boys in 1853 to Danes, Saxons, and Normans.

Forty eight chapters follow King John and the barons. A squire and a citizen open the tale, then the Tower of London, a man of the forest, and the barons in London. The day of Runnymede falls at chapter eighteen, but the story runs on. It takes in the end of King John, the coronation of the boy Henry, a sea fight, and the siege of Mount Sorrel.
49699-the-merry-andrew-or-the-humours-of:
The Merry Andrew, or the Humours of a Fair, is a small chapbook for boys. Houlston and Son printed and sold it at Wellington for two pence. Cuts, or small wood pictures, adorn its few pages through the tale. The tale gives a picture of the fun found at a country fair. It opens in a way the writer calls not at all wonderful.

Boys rush to the fair as Jack Pudding comes by with a gridiron. The tale warns small boys to keep clear of the pressing crowd. Dick Wilson thrusts into the mob and gets squeezed for his pains. Sam comes puffing in with news from the region of nonsense. A fat fellow in the crush has made Sam laugh past measure. The fun of the fair mixes with plain advice for young lads.
49979-the-master-of-stair:
The Master of Stair, by Marjorie Bowen, was published in 1907. McClure, Phillips issued the novel at New York that April. Bowen had written The Viper of Milan before. She gives this book to Mark Twain. His kind interest in a beginner's work earns her deep thanks, she writes. Two books divide the contents. Book one runs through twenty five chapters. Ronald Macdonald, a kiss, and Delia Featherstonehaugh open it. The curse of the Dalrymples is named midway. The Master himself appears at chapter eleven. William of Orange enters near the first book's end. Glencoe closes it, at chapter twenty five.

Book two is a reckoning in six chapters. The triumphs of the Campbells stand among them. One chapter denies the massacre in its title. An epilogue, The Glen o' Weeping, ends the tale.
5052-absalom-s-hair:
This novel opens with Harald Kaas at sixty, no longer living the free, uncriticized life of a bachelor. His yacht no longer sails past the coast during the summer months. His trips to England and to southern lands have come to an end. Even at his Christiania club, where his huge frame once filled the doorways, he is now seldom seen.

He was always bandy-legged, and that flaw has become more pronounced. His powerful back has curved, and he bends forward slightly. His broad forehead, which fits no hat but his own, has grown taller. Almost all his hair is gone, leaving only a straggling tuft above each ear and a sparse strip at the back. No author appears in the catalog record. Readers get a portrait of aging vanity and late love, told with Scandinavian irony.
50705-the-de-bercy-affair:
The de Bercy Affair is a detective novel by Gordon Holmes, copyrighted in 1910. Grosset and Dunlap issued the New York edition. Howard Chandler Christy drew the illustrations. Holmes had written A Mysterious Disappearance and By Force of Circumstances. The first chapter opens at New Scotland Yard. Chief Inspector Winter sits in his office among littered documents.

Winter snaps questions at a constable about a visit to a man's residence. His chewed moustache and sharp manner set his character at once. Seventeen chapters carry the case forward. A missing blade, a sun dial, a letter, and a diary mark the clues. The Saracen dagger appears as a chapter title. Osborne makes a vow before the arrests come. Two women take the field in the chapter before the closing scene.
51601-between-the-larch-woods-and-the-we:
Flora Klickmann, editor of The Girl's Own Paper and Woman's Magazine and author of The Flower-Patch among the Hills, wrote this book of country life, published at New York by Frederick Stokes. She dedicates it to the memory of her brothers Arthur, Bertie, and Wilfrid, and heads it with Wordsworth's lines on the spirit in the woods.

Her preamble sets the scene: an old cottage on a high hill above the river Wye. It stands near the very weir beside which Wordsworth sat when he wrote his famous lines. The house hides among larches, birch, oak, and wild cherry that change from spring mist to autumn copper and orange. Klickmann teases the motorists who race from Chepstow to Ross along the one good road and never spare an eye for the woods towering above them.
51788-trif-and-trixy-a-story-of-a-dreadf:
Trif and Trixy tells of a dreadfully delightful little girl and her adoring, tormented parents. John Habberton, author of Helen's Babies, wrote the tale. Altemus published the book at Philadelphia in 1897. The contents run to twenty eight chapters of family comedy.

Trixy, whose right name is Beatrice, has passed her seventh birthday. She is as wise and wild as an only child tends to become. Her people still called her the baby until her deeds checked them. Trif is her mother, who dislikes a name that hints at trifling. Chapters promise a deal in cotton, a search party, and tricks played on Trixy herself. Two more couples widen the fun beyond the nursery. Habberton writes domestic farce with a warm heart.
52248-across-south-america-an-account-of:
Hiram Bingham wrote Across South America, an account of a journey from Buenos Aires to Lima by way of Potosi. Houghton Mifflin issued it at Boston and New York in 1911, with eighty illustrations and maps. Bingham had earlier crossed Venezuela and Colombia on an expedition of 1906-07. He dedicated this volume to the mother of six little boys. The route begins at Pernambuco and Bahia, then Rio and Santos.

Buenos Aires, the Tucuman express, and the Argentine highlands come next. The party crosses the Bolivian frontier to Potosi and Sucre. Oruro, Antofagasta, and Valparaiso lead to Santiago and the first Pan-American Scientific Congress. Northern Chile and southern Peru follow, then La Paz and the Bolivia railway. Cuzco, Sacsahuaman, and the climb to Choqquequirau close the road to Lima. Bingham writes travel, trade, and ruins in one survey.
53534-josephine-e-butler-an-autobiograph:
Johnson and co-editor shaped this memoir of reformer Josephine Butler from her words. Arrowsmith and Simpkin printed the second impression in 1909. Stuart adds a front essay on her life and work. A Richmond portrait of Butler about 1852 fronts the book.

Editors call her one of the noblest women who ever lived. They draw chiefly on her Recollections of George Butler memoir. Personal Reminiscences of a Great Crusade adds much material here. No private letters stand in the book, by her strong wish. Stuart front essay and the editors thread hold her own words in one clear line.
5589-the-elixir:
Georg Ebers wrote The Elixir as a true story centered on a tall gabled house in Leipzig's Katherinenstrasse, not far from the Market Place. The house has belonged to his family for a long time, and many curious things happened there worthy of rescue from oblivion. Though relatives would now like to relieve him of the task, Ebers insists on telling what he found.

The tale follows the house's secrets, with an elixir at its heart promising more than medicine. Ebers writes family history as mystery. Readers get a short, curious story of old Leipzig, where a family house keeps its wonders close.
56660-you-re-on-the-air:
You're on the Air is a boys' novel by William Heyliger, published in New York by Appleton-Century in 1941. Neil O'Keeffe illustrated the book. The title points to radio, the new stage for its young hero.

A frontispiece caption shows the world of the story. One character tells another that he has been first an actor and now a producer, and suggests script writing next. The publisher's list at the front links the novel to Heyliger's sports books and his Don Strong scout series. The copyright page notes an earlier serial copyright of 1940. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg, its fiction notice intact.
56838-the-saintsbury-affair:
Roman Doubleday wrote this detective novel, published by Little, Brown in 1912, by the author of The Hemlock Avenue Mystery. Its narrator dates the tangle from a telephone invitation to dinner at Mrs Whyte's.

She has a charming young guest, Miss Katherine Thurston, and wants him at his most agreeable. The contents promise two lovely ladies, crossed wires, and Bertillon methods among others. A frat supper, a simmering samovar, and the trail of Diavolo follow; the samovar explodes. Later chapters bring tangled heart-strings, an outlaw, a gift-bond, and the ultimate discovery. The frontispiece shows a chatelaine purse emptied onto a waiter's tray. Readers get a society mystery with dinner-party banter and Continental shadows.
57136-science-from-an-easy-chair:
Science from an Easy Chair collects forty-three popular essays by Sir Ray Lankester. Methuen published it in London, first on April 14, 1910. This second edition followed in May 1910. Eighty-four illustrations accompany the text. Lankester had written Extinct Animals and The Kingdom of Man. The essays range across the whole of natural science.

Darwin opens the volume, in three essays on the theory and its defence. Metchnikoff and Tolstoi share a chapter. Fresh-water jelly-fishes and the story of the common eel follow. Modern horses and their ancestors get an essay of their own. The dragon is weighed as fancy or fact. Oysters, sleep, and the heart's beat treat the body. Protoplasm and the simplest living things treat life's basis. Cholera, death-rates, and the feeble-minded bring in public health. Protective colouring, the phylloxera, and clothes moths cover pests. Cave-men and the Neander men close the book.
57663-historical-record-of-the-sixty-sev:
Historical Record of the Sixty-Seventh, or the South Hampshire Regiment, tells the life of one British regiment from its raising in 1758 to the year 1849. Richard Cannon compiled it at the Adjutant-General's Office at Horse Guards, and it was printed at London in 1849. The book carries plates of the regiment's dress and colours.

The colour bears a royal tiger with the word India, for service there from 1805 to 1826. It also bears Barrosa, for the gallantry of the second battalion on March 5, 1811, and Peninsula, for service in the east of Spain. Cannon's set aimed to give each regiment in the Queen's service the same full record.
58125-colonel-henry-ludington-a-memoir:
Willis Fletcher Johnson's Colonel Henry Ludington: A Memoir was printed at New York in 1907 by the colonel's grandchildren, Lavinia Elizabeth Ludington and Charles Henry Ludington. Portraits, views, and facsimiles crowd the book. The frontispiece shows the grist mill Ludington built at Fredericksburgh, now Kent, about the time of the Revolution.

Chapters run from the family line through the years before the Revolution, the war itself, secret service work, and service between the lines. The plates give the paper trail of a militia colonel. His captain's commission from Governor Tryon stands there, and his colonel's commissions of 1776 and 1778, with letters and arrest orders from the Committee on Conspiracies. Later generations of the family close the memoir.
58612-the-ornithologist-and-oo-logist-vo:
The Ornithologist and Oölogist for March 1883 is a number of the Boston bird journal edited by Wade, volume eight, number three, priced at ten cents. The journal served the egg-collecting and bird-watching culture of the eighteen eighties. Its leading article, Among the Buteos, reviews the breeding habits of the New England hawks from the writer's notes.

The writer claims his ground round Norwich as the home of the Buteos: he took 104 eggs in a season, and sixty were taken or destroyed around him. Sixteen pairs of red-shouldered hawks bred within a line drawn outside the suburbs. The secret is food: red squirrels swarm in the nut-bearing groves, and hawk nests are provisioned with them by the dozen, nine squirrel portions in one red-tail's nest. The article is ornithology of the collecting era, precise, local and unembarrassed about the taking.
59558-your-servant-sir:
Your Servant, Sir, a science fiction tale by Sol Boren, ran in Worlds of If in October 1956. The blurb asks what a civilized man can do when his perfect android servant drives him crazy with blunt talk. The tale opens as Paula Golden, suitcase in hand, tells her husband Raymond that she is leaving.

The android stares and tells Paula, in a perfect voice, that she is getting quite fat. When she storms out, it adds that her dress is atrocious and she should change to a gray one at once. Raymond grips his glass and begs her to wait while he gets the machine fixed, sold, or traded. Boren plays the clash for sharp, sour comedy.
59670-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Upton Sinclair. The index lists the tales and essays held in that library, with their tables of contents. The Jungle heads the list, with its thirty-one chapters.

Damaged Goods, a novel made from a play by Eugene Brieux, comes next. The Profits of Religion follows, with its books on the church of the conquerors and the church of good society. Chapter heads there run from The Priestly Lie to Hell-Fire. King Midas, The Metropolis, and Jimmie Higgins stand among the novels. King Coal, Samuel the Seeker, and Love's Pilgrimage are also listed. The index serves readers hunting Sinclair's works.
60125-the-winding-stair:
The Winding Stair is a novel of Morocco by Mason, author of The Four Feathers. Doran held the rights in 1923, and Grosset and Dunlap issued this edition at New York. A film plate from the screen version faces the title page. Bacon's line on rising by a winding stair stands as motto.

The tale opens in a London lawyer's office on a Friday evening. Ferguson longs for his garden at Goring and a day on the links. His clerk insists he look at one more visitor's card. From that refusal the plot unwinds toward North Africa. Chapters promise a villa, a sacred city, and companions of the night. A captain's report and a coup de grace mark the crisis. Mason wrote of empire's edges, where a man's past climbs the stair behind him.
60568-the-fishdollar-affair:
McKenna wrote this science fiction story for Worlds of If in October 1958. Its blurb calls the tale tender, ironic and funny, and names its hero an ensign of more courage than prudence. Ensign Stephen Welnicki serves as watch officer on Galactic Patrol Ship Carlyle, cruising through subspace without boredom.

The ship's computer turns fields and shifts twenty-seven variables by threes, leaving Welnicki idle and free to think. He wonders whether a never-found alien mind might live in subspace itself. Weird things, eating mathematics and fighting with music, fill his fancy, until command of the ship in a crisis becomes his daydream.
6082-our-pilots-in-the-air:
Captain William B. Perry sets Our Pilots in the Air in eastern France, not far from No Man's Land, where low hills enclose broad levels and a creek poetically called a river. The striking feature is a Flying Camp on trampled greensward, ringed by high board walls in an irregular oval, with hangars, roadways, and a clump of trees.

Young men in khaki and aviator caps gather at a bulletin board, reading a placard for Bombing Squadron members to be on the qui vive. Perry writes of bombing air raids, squadron life, and the humor of young fliers. The camp itself, queer-shaped buildings and all, becomes a character in the war story.
61166-the-story-of-a-peninsular-veteran-:
A sergeant in the Forty-third Light Infantry tells his own story in this account of the Peninsular War, printed in London. The writer says he owes the facts of battles and sieges to Napier's history of the war. A portrait of Arthur, Duke of Wellington, fronts the book. The contents run to eleven chapters, with views of Arklow, Copenhagen, and Corunna among the pictures.

The writer, Thomas, was the youngest of six children, born in King's County in Ireland about the year 1790. Chapter One tells of the Irish rebellion, the action at Arklow, and his entry into the army. Pictures of the storming of Ciudad Rodrigo and the castle of Badajos point to the hard fighting ahead in Spain.
6166-charles-lamb-a-memoir:
Barry Cornwall, in his seventy-seventh year, records recollections of Charles Lamb, believing himself nearly the only man surviving who knew much of the excellent Elia. He knew Lamb more intimately than any other living person during the last seventeen or eighteen years of his life.

Proud to join his name with Lamb's, Cornwall recalls former times to bring his old friend before a new generation. He asks the courteous reader to accept desultory labors of a lover of letters, hoping modern advocates will admit his recollections of a fine genius departed. No harm, and possibly benefit, may follow wider acquaintance with England's rare humorist.
61795-from-an-easy-chair:
From an Easy Chair gathers short, plain-spoken pieces on science by the zoologist Ray Lankester, issued by Constable in London in 1909 after a first appearance the year before. Written for general readers, the pieces take up whatever caught a working scientist's eye, from laboratory research to odd sights reported in the news.

The contents range widely: work at the Pasteur Institute, the sea serpent, giraffes and the okapi, diamonds, and the great geologists. Other pieces treat malaria, Malta fever, a cure for sleeping sickness, tsetse flies, the house-fly, colour photography, and photographs of Mars. Luminous owls, rats and plague, ancient temples, tobacco, votes for women, and memories of Kelvin fill out the list. The pieces show how a leading biologist explained new findings to the public in an age when science writing reached most readers through print.
61989-some-artists-at-the-fair:
Some Artists at the Fair is a set of pieces on the great fair of 1893. Five men of art and craft wrote the pieces for this book. It came out in New York in the year of the fair itself. The fair was the World's Fair held in the town of Chicago.

Its great court and dome stand at the front of the book as a plate. The writers praise the grand style and fine scale of the halls. They feel awe at the charm of the place as they walk its grounds. They feel grief too, that the halls are not built to last past the fair. The pieces take the dress of the grounds, the types of its guests. The art of the white town and its fair views fill the rest. Plates of dome art and carved forms dress the book throughout.
62811-our-western-hills-how-to-reach-the:
Our Western Hills is a walking guide by an unnamed Glasgow pedestrian. Morison Brothers published the shilling book at Glasgow in 1892. The full title promises how to reach the hills and what may be seen from their summits. A letter at the front dedicates the pages to the man who suggested them.

The writer offers the guide to working folk for holidays and Saturday afternoons. He claims no fine writing and no new matter, only a clear path to the hilltops. The hills chosen lie within reach of any walker of average strength. Notes tell what can be seen from each top and nearby. He grants that Scotland lacks the solemn look of the Alps. Yet he praises the colour, size, and shape of the home hills, and their ties to history.
62962-autographs-for-freedom-by-mrs-harr:
Autographs for Freedom is an anti-slavery gift book edited for the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society. It was published in London in 1853. Harriet Beecher Stowe heads a list of thirty-six writers who gave pieces to the cause. The English preface praises the leading minds of America for setting their hands to a solemn protest against slavery.

Stowe stands in the company of Horace Mann, the poet Whittier, and Frederick Douglass. Douglass had himself lived the horrors the book condemns. Such autograph albums were sold and given to raise money and feeling for abolition. This one joins famous names to short pieces against the system of slavery.
63122-geography-of-the-air:
Geography of the Air is an annual report by Greely, vice-president for that subject in the National Geographic Society. It was presented to the Society on January 23, 1891, and printed in The National Geographic Magazine for May 1, 1891, priced at twenty-five cents. Greely owns that his official duties left him less time for the report than the subject merited.

He notes a year rich in argument about weather science, with writers in split branches of the field trying to reconcile their views. Some, he says, still grope in the first, fact gathering stage of the science. The report takes up the genesis of storms and the general circulation of the atmosphere, weighing fresh claims with care.
65032-wind-in-her-hair:
Wind in Her Hair is a science fiction story by Kris Neville. It appeared in Imagination in October 1950. A headnote introduces its two young leads. To Marte and Johnny Nine the spaceship was their world. Yet they dreamed of returning home to an Earth they had never seen.

The tale opens below the ship's giant atomic motors. Johnny calls for Marte on the last level. She hides in shadow by their special bulb. She hopes each day that he will come. Fear troubles her talk, though. The return seems too good to happen. She begs him to say that nothing will go wrong. He says it slowly, word by word. The story dwells on the two young people and their dread.
65737-light-ho-sir:
Frank Bullen, author of The Cruise of the Cachalot, published these sea pieces with Crowell at New York in 1901. The title story and My Night Watch Is Over are tales of conversion. Bullen opens with an argument. Students of human nature, he says, love to trace every change in a man to his early training. They ignore the doctrine of the New Birth, and their method, he charges, is dishonest.

His proof is a sailor who had never, until the time of the story, received the remotest idea of the relations of God to man. To such a one, Bullen writes, the water of the Word comes like the monsoon rains on the burnt-up breadths of India, and the dead soil puts on living green at once. Bullen had lived his conversion at sea, and his tracts carried a forecastle accent no pulpit could imitate.
66446-the-plymouth-express-affair:
The Plymouth Express Affair is a mystery story by Agatha Christie featuring her detective Hercule Poirot. A headnote praises the little grey cells Poirot so often speaks of. The tale opens on a December night at Newton Abbot station.

A young naval officer boards a first-class compartment of the Plymouth Express with a heavy suitcase. The carriage is his alone as the train pulls out. A strange smell makes him frown, and he knows it at once for chloroform. He opens his suitcase, takes out papers and magazines, and settles to smoke. The woman later found dead in the train hangs over the quiet scene. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
66751-the-heir:
The Heir, a novel by Sydney C Grier, was published by William Blackwood and Sons in 1906, with pictures by George Percy Jacomb-Hood. It stands first in the Balkan Series, second part. Grier also wrote An Uncrowned King and The Warden of the Marches. Claims to a throne drive the tale.

Chapter heads promise a legal claim, a stock of emperors, and a ride on the Orient Express. A jewel case, a trap, and a night's lodging follow. Maurice and Eirene are the young leads; an illustration shows Maurice gripped by brigands beside her horse. A parchment scroll and the girdle of Isidora carry the secret of birth. Unmasking, bribery, and a fusion of interests close the intrigue.
66840-the-autobiography-of-upton-sinclai:
Upton Sinclair told his own story for Harcourt, Brace and World at New York. He had written for seventy-one years, he says, having started at thirteen. Readers had long asked for the life, and halfway through he had answered with American Outpost. The major part of that book, revised, is folded into this volume. Sinclair casts himself as a veteran of campaigns, gathering youngsters about his knee in a light tone.

The contents run from childhood and youth through genius, marriage, revolt, and utopia. Wandering and exile follow, then a new beginning and the road west to California. The Muckrake Man takes up The Jungle years; EPIC recalls the campaign for governor; Lanny Budd brings the novels of the second fame. Photographs show him with Shaw, London, Eisenstein, and Einstein. His 250,000 letters, he notes, wait at the Lilly Library in Indiana for readers not satisfied.
67280-the-history-of-the-lady-betty-stai:
Molly Elliot Seawell's The History of the Lady Betty Stair was published by Scribner's of New York in 1897, with drawings by Thule de Thulstrup. The frontispiece shows a cross given for tried bravery, with the words, None has deserved it more than you. Seawell had already written Children of Destiny and Throckmorton.

The tale opens in 1798 at the palace of Holyrood, filled with French exiles around the Comte d'Artois, the future Charles the Tenth. Four lives meet there that had crossed long before at Versailles: an old priest who was once a soldier, the charming De Bourmont, the handsome scoundrel Bastien, and Lady Betty herself. Betty had known both men in 1789, when she was a girl of fifteen.
68045-she-and-he-lavinia-memoir:
She and He, and Lavinia gathers two tales by George Sand in one volume. Burnham Ives turned the French tales into English for this edition. Burgan wrote the memoir of the author that stands before the tales. Barrie and Son of Philadelphia printed the book for subscribers only. Six photogravures after paintings and a portrait stand through the volume.

The memoir tells of Amandine Dupin, Baroness Dudevant, called George Sand. She was born in Paris on July 5, in the year 1804. Her father came of aristocratic birth, her mother of humbler stock. A corner at the opera ball fronts the first of the tales. Thérèse hears her name spoken by the man she loved so well. Laurent paints Palmer's portrait in another of the pictured scenes. Their first supper, a fantastic vision, and the separation follow on. Lionel surprises Lavinia in the second tale's pictured moment.
68153-the-step-on-the-stair:
The Step on the Stair is a tale of crime by Anna Katharine Green, the hand of a famed case of a great hall. Her past tales are named on the title leaf. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty three. The front plate shows a rough draw plan shown to a court room. Its list of parts falls in four books with short names.

The three men of one name head the first book. Hid is the name of the next. Which of us two is the name of the third. Love is the name of the last. The tale opens on a street of the great town. I had turn the bend at a street of the town, the teller says.
69473-the-life-of-cardinal-mezzofanti-wi:
The Life of Cardinal Mezzofanti is a biography by Russell, president of Saint Patrick's College, Maynooth, printed in London in 1858. An introductory memoir of eminent linguists, ancient and modern, stands before the life. Mezzofanti was the most famous polyglot of his age. A portrait after Perugini fronts the volume.

The memoir grew from an article in the Edinburgh Review of 1855. The subject excited considerable interest at the time. The article was translated into French and, abridged, into Italian. Strangers wrote to Russell through the editor, urging him to complete the biography and offering fresh information. The notices then existing were all his materials, and they seemed thin for a life. He set out to gather, while they were still recent, the memories of persons of many countries and tongues who had known and spoken with the Cardinal. The book is the fruit of that harvest.
69515-in-the-tiger-s-lair:
Leo Miller, who wrote In the Wilds of South America, sent his hunters back to Inca country in this sequel tale. Scribner printed In the Tiger's Lair at New York in 1921, with plates by Paul Bransom. Miller gives it to the memory of little Robert.

Quizquiz, Inca, Child of the Sun, commands that you appear before his sacred person: the front plate's line sets the stakes. The end of the underground river opens the road. A return to the land of the Incas and a rivalry of airmen follow. The hunt for hidden treasure brings the crowning misfortune. In the tiger's lair, the Inca's threat, and Soncco's shrewdness fill the middle. The prisoners capture the king at last.
69682-tom-swift-circling-the-globe-or-th:
Tom Swift Circling the Globe is a boys' adventure novel by Victor Appleton, published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1927. It stands late in the long Tom Swift series, after the airline express volume. Tom's new machine is the Air Monarch, built for a cruise around the world.

The contents promise a fast start: a blast of fire, then Tom accepts the challenge. A nose dive and a rescue follow before the flight begins. Chapters carry the Air Monarch across the ocean, forced down, and through a hurricane. Whizzing bullets and a rescue at the midpoint keep the pace up. Series fiction of this kind sold invention as adventure. Each volume gave boy readers a new machine and a race against trouble. This one sends the young inventor around the whole globe by air.
6981-the-open-air:
Richard Jefferies collects papers on the open air, first printed in the Standard, Longman's Magazine, the Manchester Guardian, and other journals. The contents range from Saint Guido and golden brown wild flowers to sunny Brighton, the pine wood, and nature on the roof. One of the new voters, the modern Thames, the single barrel gun, and the haunt of the hare sit beside the bathing season, downs, and forest beauty.

Later pieces follow February out of doors, haunts of the lapwing, the London road, red roofs, and a wet night in London. Saint Guido opens with a boy running out at a garden gate into a sandy lane and up a grassy bank to a footpath. Jefferies writes nature with a close eye and a poet's sense of light and season.
70066-twenty-years-a-fakir:
Twenty Years a Fakir is a rogue's memoir printed at Omaha, Nebraska, in 1899 by the Gate City Book and Novelty Company, priced at fifty cents. Its writer signs himself only with initials, and a Byron line stands on the cover: those who would be free must strike the blow themselves. A fakir, in his trade tongue, is a street seller who works crowds with schemes and patter.

The contents roll out the trade: starting out as a hotel porter, selling cards, lightning rods, soap, and pens on the street.
