Later chapters give the soap racket, auction gags, a museum scheme, and travel without paying railroad fare. The writer tells of free lunches, low ebbs, and being not only broke but dead broke.
70787-under-the-absolute-amir:
Frank Martin wrote Under the Absolute Amir, published by Harper and Brothers in London and New York in 1907. Martin served for eight years as engineer-in-chief to two amirs of Afghanistan, Abdur Rahman and Habibullah. For most of that time he was the only Englishman in Kabul. His book, illustrated with his own drawings and photographs, opens with a portrait of Amir Habibullah Khan.

The early chapters follow the road to Kabul: the order of march, pack animals, camps, and the cold march by way of Ghazni. Martin describes Kabul itself in detail, its bazars, streets, guest-house, and baths. He records his reception by the Amir and the look of the palace and audience chamber. Later chapters treat manners and customs. Few Europeans had lived at the Afghan court, and Martin's account remains a rare inside record of the country under its absolute rulers.
71155-facing-the-chair:
John Dos Passos wrote a plea book for two men set to die in the chair. The Sacco-Vanzetti Defense Committee put it out in Boston in 1927. Its theme is how two foreign-born work men were made American. A plea quote at the front warns of rule by fear. Anatole France's call to the American folk opens the case.

France holds the two were doomed for a crime of thought. Thompson's plea for a fresh trial is quoted at length. Dos Passos tells their lives as work men in a new land. The book asks if law served truth or scorn of the strange. Its tone is grave, hot, and full of dread. Case fans get the defense view in full.
71213-adventures-of-the-runaway-rocking-:
Howard R Garis wrote Adventures of the Runaway Rocking Chair, a tale for young children. Grosset and Dunlap issued the book in nineteen hundred twenty six. Lang Campbell drew the pictures. The tale stands in the Happy Home Series of child tales.

Racky, a fine brown rocking chair with four legs, starts the fun. Nat and Weezie, his small friends, play at Happy Home. Grandma Harden owns the house next door on the lane. Rodney and Addie live there, with Thump the dog. Racky runs away in the first tale and trails scrapes. A snow storm, a lost doll, and Santa Claus fill later parts. The last tale, Rattle Bang, winds the chair’s wild year. Garis of Uncle Wiggily fame keeps each scrap short and gay.
7149-the-poetical-works-of-henry-kirk-wh:
Henry Kirke White's poetical works appear here with a memoir by Sir Harris Nicolas, inscribed to Peter Smith in testimony of esteem and friendship. Miscellaneous poems open with Clifton Grove, Time, and Childhood in two parts, then the Christiad and lines on a survey of the heavens. Lines supposed to be spoken by a lover at his mistress's grave, My Study, and a description of a summer's eve follow.

Lines bidding the raging sea be still, verses written in the prospect of death, and verses on pride, envy, and scorn sit beside a fragment on Pandora's fatal train. Loud rage the winds without, a wintry cloud, and lines to a friend in distress come next. Christmas Day leads to Nelson, an epigram on Bloomfield, and an elegy for Gill, drowned in the Trent while bathing. The memoir frames a young poet's brief life.
72651-may-fair:
Michael Arlen, who wrote The Green Hat, gathered these tales of smart London in May Fair. Doran printed it at New York in 1925, with a jacket by Edmund Dulac. Arlen calls the book the last adventures of these charming people.

His long subtitle promises the real state of things in London's heart. The years are the fifteenth and sixteenth of King George the Fifth's reign. Falls, fights, and flirts of the smart set fill the bill. The Revolting Doom of a Gentleman Who Would Not Dance with His Wife heads the list. The Battle of Berkeley Square, the Ace of Cads, and the Ghoul of Golders Green keep the tone: bright, sharp, and a touch cruel.
72715-harry-muir:
Harry Muir, A Story of Scottish Life, is a three volume novel of 1853, printed in London by Hurst and Blackett. Its author was already known for Passages in the Life of Mrs Margaret Maitland. An epigraph from King Henry the Fourth sets the theme of a young man's bright hopes and threatened fall.

The first chapter opens in the crypt of Glasgow cathedral, where a guide shows young visitors the pillar where Rob Roy hid. One grave young man wanders off alone, already marked by the thoughtfulness that drives the tale. The book belongs to the rich Scots domestic school that made everyday provincial life carry real moral weight.
72777-harry-muir:
Harry Muir, a story of Scottish life, was written by the author of Passages in the Life of Mrs Margaret Maitland. Hurst and Blackett published it at London in 1853, in three volumes; this is the second. A motto from King Henry the Fourth heads the title, on Harry's ruined hopes. The volume opens in Edinburgh, at the house of Mrs Charteris. Her son Cuthbert, an advocate, has come back from an errand.

Cuthbert presents his friend Harry Muir, who will bear that name only a day or two longer. He was right after all, and the old lady owns her prophecy of failure wrong. She welcomes Harry to Edinburgh and wishes him joy of his inheritance. Mrs Charteris warms to the stranger as he leans toward Cuthbert, his guide and counsellor.
73086-harry-muir:
Harry Muir, a story of Scottish life, closes with this third volume, printed in London in 1853. Hurst and Blackett issued the set, by the author of the Maitland tale and Merkland. A line from King Henry the Fourth stands as the book's warning motto.

The volume opens on the eve of a great party, with Cuthbert Charteris arriving at Allenders. Half frozen from his ride, he shakes snow from his coat into a warm dining room. Harry had met him in Stirling and driven him out through the December night. Agnes, bright and welcoming, tells of an unexpected call from young Dunlop. His sister, a baronet's daughter, may grace the party, to the house's delight. Agnes had dared the invitation only at the last moment, with faint hope of success. Rose and Martha are with the visitor as the news spreads.
73177-cool-air:
Cool Air is a tale of horror by Lovecraft. The Project Gutenberg text was taken from Weird Tales for September 1939. Its headnote calls it a tale of dark science, and of the mystery that hung round a Spanish doctor's work with cold air.

The narrator begins by owning his dread. He shivers more than other men in a cold room, and feels sick when the chill of evening creeps through a mild day. He says the fear began in a shabby rooming house in New York. In the spring of 1923 he was doing poor magazine work and drifting from one cheap lodging to the next. A brownstone house in West Fourteenth Street pleased him better than the rest. What he met there, in full daylight and city noise, is the horror he sets out to tell.
7396-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
The Iron Gate, the title poem of this volume, was read at a breakfast given in Holmes's honor, and it sets the mood for poems of 1877 to 1881. The gate stands for the threshold of old age, and the poems that follow look backward and forward from it: Vestigia, My Aviary, On the Threshold, and Rhymes of a Life-time. Tributes appear for Whittier's seventieth birthday and for the Moore centennial.

Holmes also welcomes a Chicago club, celebrates Harvard and the American Academy, and writes of home and country in the centennial's wake. The verse is quieter than his early work, more meditative, with the wit softened into reflection. Readers who know the Autocrat will find the same mind here, older now, measuring a life in poems.
74130-prize-of-the-air:
Prize of the Air is a flight tale by Ben Conlon of sky men and cash. Bill Barlow loops at two thou feet with a fare man in seat two at start. He banks left on a cut mill and lands dead stick at his set mark. The field chief runs up mad, since loop with a fare breaks field law. Saxton paid five hundred dollars for that loop, Barlow grins back.

His fare fly card is torn up on the spot for that stunt. Barlow minds it not, a man who laughs at death scorns such loss. Saxton then bids him fly him home to Pampa in New Mexico fast. Trains are too slow for his age, the rich fare man tells him. That bid sets the long flight plot of the tale in train.
74171-cities-in-the-air:
Edmond Hamilton wrote Cities in the Air, a serial in an air magazine of 1929. It ran in the November and December numbers of that year. The editors call it one of the most striking tales they have read. For audacity and adventure it stands foremost, they say. Advances in flying point the way to its wonders, they add.

Planes have stayed in the air for weeks without coming down, they note. Buildings now house forty thousand people at one time on earth. Soon single buildings will house a hundred thousand and more, they hold. Life at the surface is unhealthy with dust and dense air, they argue. Lung diseases thrive there, while high altitudes clear them away. Doctors already send the afflicted to higher air, the editors say. An order to Captain Brant from the first air chief opens the war of the sky cities.
7445-ars-recte-vivendi-being-essays-cont:
George William Curtis wrote the Easy Chair essays for Harper's Magazine, and this collection gathers about a dozen of them under a Latin title meaning the art of living rightly. A college professor had suggested the gathering, saying these essays so nearly cover the vital questions of hygiene, courtesy, and morality that they deserved a volume of their own.

The contents live up to that praise in a practical way. There are essays on extravagance at college, brains and brawn, hazing, the soul of the gentleman, theatre manners, woman's dress, and secret societies. Curtis writes as a friendly counselor, not a preacher, on how to behave decently in a busy republic. The book is a Victorian manual of manners with a conscience.
7453-the-dialect-of-the-west-of-england-:
James Jennings, honorary secretary of the Metropolitan Literary Institution in London, made this record of the speech of the West of England, particularly Somersetshire. The book gives a glossary of words now in use there, together with poems and other pieces that exemplify the dialect in action. A farewell poem in the old spelling opens the volume, with its wild notes and rustic rhymes.

The edition here is the second, revised and corrected by a relative, James Knight Jennings, who added observations from several years' residence in the center of the district. For readers of Hardy and the West Country novelists, the glossary unlocks a whole world of local speech. For linguists, it is an early, careful record of a dialect before radio and schooling smoothed it away.
74709-a-knight-of-the-air:
Henry Coxwell's Knight of the Air, or the Aerial Rivals, was published by Digby, Long in London. Publisher's lists front the volume: Digby's Popular Novel Series at two shillings sixpence a volume, and pages of praise for Arabella Kenealy's novels. Coxwell was known for My Life and Balloon Experiences. A picture caption gives the book's flavour: just as the pilot and Bennet began winding down the balloon, a gun's report was heard. That scene falls at page 156 of the tale.

The series list prices picture-board editions at two shillings and names Marryat, Russell, Meade, and Nisbet among its authors. Coxwell brought a working balloonist's knowledge to his fiction. Rivalry in the air, in the early days of ballooning contests, drives the plot. The book is a popular novel of its decade, dressed for the railway bookstall. Its front matter is itself a small archive of eighteen-nineties publishing.
76331-the-motion-picture-chums-at-the-fa:
The Motion Picture Chums at the Fair is a boys' series novel by Victor Appleton. Grosset and Dunlap issued it in New York in 1915. Its subtitle promises the greatest film ever exhibited. The heroes run a moving picture theatre on upper Broadway. The first chapter shows them counting a pile of bills and silver. Hard times do not seem to touch their trade. Randy Powell and Pep Smith voice the hope and the fear.

The contents list runs to twenty-five chapters. A collision and a rescue open the action. The chums then plan a trip to a great fair. Wild life films and a wonderful film reel follow. A theft and a recovery stir the close. Success is the final chapter's name. Appleton's shop wrote series books to a house plan. This one rides the new craze for the movies.
77176-in-mid-air:
In Mid-Air is a war tale by R. J. McSwiney. Its head note states its knot: a wartime flyer, unable to land without killing himself, decides to die in glory. The tale opens at six thousand feet, by the dial of the plane. The goal below was already taking clear form in the blurred land.

A cluster of drab canvas buildings stood out, hard to make out against the sea of mud round them. That was all that could yet be seen of the airfield picked for that morning's bomb raid into the foe's lines. It was a chill winter morning, the tale says. Low clouds ran swift across a gray sky: fine weather for such a task. The squadron flew high and changed course when the clouds came between it and the guns below.
77315-the-chateau-of-montplaisir:
The Chateau of Montplaisir is a novel of France by Molly Elliot Seawell. Appleton published the book at New York in 1906. Seawell had written The Sprightly Romance of Marsac and Papa Bouchard. Nine chapters carry the tale from a rain swept coast to a merry week in Paris.

Louis Victor de Latour has just inherited the chateau of Montplaisir. He sits glum at a window of its great saloon, watching rain drip through the glass dome. The vast pile stands cracked and half boarded, its court choked with broken stone. Latour was the merriest of fellows while poor, the narrator says. Wealth in this form has made him sad as an owl. An uncle, an aunt, and a niece soon join the dance of the plot.
77592-buckin-the-air:
Buckin' the Air is a rodeo tale by Bud La Mar, illustrated by Frank Hoban. Its billing promises the wild adventure of two demon rodeo-riders who dare a new element in an airplane. The narrator and Bearcat Gibson were the happiest cowboys this side of Denver. After a long spell of hard luck they had sneaked up on the rest of the boys and won most of the prize money at the Eldora rodeo.

On the last day of the Eldora show came a letter from their old pal Clay Hinkle. Clay had been elected head judge of the San Dominick Rodeo. He had not forgot the time they got him out of jail in Berryville, and he offers them a share in the first and second money in the bronc riding. A passage preserved in the copy gives the catch.
777-the-mastery-of-the-air:
William J. Claxton wrote this popular history of flight for readers who want the story, not the sums. He states plainly that he does not dwell on technical science, but on the real deeds of pioneers who made aviation what it is. Balloons, gliders, and early aeroplanes all find a place, with the men who flew them.

Claxton writes with enthusiasm for brave trial and error, from first hops to long flights. His aim is to stir an intelligent interest in the art of flying, and he succeeds by keeping the human tale to the fore. The book is a friendly guide to the heroic age of the air, suited to young readers and general fans alike.
77930-mop-fair:
Mop Fair, by Arthur Binstead, was published in 1905. Sands issued it at Edinburgh and London. Binstead was known as Pitcher of the sporting paper Pink 'Un. Its subtitle offers elegant extracts from private letters. The writer is Lady Viola Drumcree, fatherless daughter of Feodorovna, Countess of Chertsey. Twelve epistles make the volume. The first is dated at Eaton Square on a Tuesday in June. Viola writes to her dearest Patricia on her nineteenth birthday.

The day was joyless, she owns, for want of a father's love. Her mother married Cecil Contango long after Viola's birth. Social duties have kept the countess too busy to name the father even now. School days at a Swiss boarding school bind the two friends. Binstead writes society satire in a girl's gushing hand.
77959-the-gold-of-ophir:
Gwinn's adventure novel, published by Neely at London and New York with copyright in 1898, is narrated by Thomas Hardman of Chicago. Hardman opens by marvelling that men still living remember Chicago as a hamlet of a dozen shops sunken in quagmire. He had no fortune but his University of Chicago education. Salaam, the first chapter, sets him toward the West.

The contents chart the romance: Leadville, a brace of mining experts, a partner taken, and a flight from the Piutes. Then come rapids to shoot, gold found, and stranger things: the Lost Tribes, the story of the tablets, a Temple of the Sun, and the chariots of Israel. Children of the Sun people the hidden land. A farewell to Ophir and a last chapter, Thornless Roses, bring the treasure tale home. It is a lost-world Western with a biblical engine.
780-the-war-in-the-air:
H. G. Wells imagined a war fought from the sky, before aeroplanes had truly arrived. Bert Smallways, a small Englishman with a love of machines, is swept up by a balloon into a German air fleet bound for America. The fleet attacks New York, and the world falls into a war of airships, bombs, and ruin.

Wells follows Bert from fleet to island to a broken world, where empires collapse and men live by scraps. The novel is both adventure and warning: new weapons, he argues, will outrun old politics. Written in 1908, it startled readers with its picture of aerial war, and it still reads as a grim, prescient fable.
7835-lothair:
Benjamin Disraeli's Lothair, in eighty-eight chapters, opens with a duchess recalling a shy pretty boy brought by his mother, once her bridesmaid. From that small memory grows a vast novel of a young lord, heir to wealth, courted by church, party, and society, each seeking to claim his soul.

Through London salons, Roman intrigue, and political salons, Lothair weighs faith, nation, and self against glittering temptations. Disraeli, himself a prime minister and novelist, writes with insider wit about power, religion, and youth, in a romance that mirrors Victorian England's great debates.
78654-the-biography-and-typography-of-wi:
William Blades wrote The Biography and Typography of William Caxton, England’s first printer. Scribner and Welford issued this second edition in New York in eighteen hundred eighty two. Blades first told the tale in two quarto books of the sixties. A cut form for the Caxton year of eighteen hundred seventy seven came next.

Caxton was born in the Weald of Kent of old stock, Blades argues. John Large, a London mercer, took the lad as his bound prentice. Bruges then claimed him for the Merchant Adventurers’ proud band. He rose to govern that band and treat for trade with dukes. Margaret of York’s great wedding graced his years in that gay town. There he turned Le Recueil into English with his own hand. Edward the Fourth, a fugitive king, took shelter in Bruges then. Print lore at root touches each art of that age, Blades holds.
78707-upton-sinclair:
Floyd Dell wrote Upton Sinclair, a Study in Social Protest, dated nineteen twenty-seven. Dell gave the book to Joseph Freeman. A photo of Sinclair by Odiorne faces the title page.

Dell opens with a puzzle: Sinclair is famed abroad as America's leading writer, yet held lower at home. The world, Dell says, sought a true account of industrial America and found it in Sinclair. Chapters run from southern beginnings through The Jungle and King Coal. Jimmie Higgins, the great pamphlets, and Oil get full treatment. A list of Sinclair's works and an index close the study. Dell writes as an ally and critic.
79652-all-s-fair:
All's Fair is a western story by Ray Humphreys, author of By Hook or by Cook. It opens in the office of the sheriff of Monte Vista. Sheriff Joe Cook has the blues, and his young deputy, Shorty McKay, comes in whistling. Shorty advises him to store his potato crop rather than sell at a loss.

Shorty also offers to catch a smart crook named Foxy Fromera himself, so the boss can go fishing. The sheriff answers with growing wrath at the cheek of the plan. The tale is told in dialect, with the dry humour of the pulp western. Its plot turns on the deputy's hunt for the crook and the sheriff's money troubles.
845-poems-of-henry-timrod-with-memoir:
Henry Timrod wrote these poems of the American South, gathered here with a memoir by Judge George S. Bryan. Spring, The Cotton Boll, and A Year's Courtship head a set that sings of fields, seasons, and young love, while later poems face war and loss. Timrod, called the laureate of the Confederacy, wrote with grace under hardship.

The memoir traces his life, poverty, and early death, and it helps readers hear the man behind the verse. His poems are musical and tender, rooted in Carolina soil. The volume preserves a Southern voice of the Civil War era, valued for its lyric beauty more than for its politics.
8600-l-assommoir:
Emile Zola's L'Assommoir follows Gervaise, a young woman in working-class Paris, from the night she waits up until two in the morning for her lover Lantier. Shivering at the window in a thin jacket, cheeks wet with tears, she watches him slip into a dance hall instead of coming home with work. The novel tracks her hopes of a clean, honest life through laundry work, marriage, and a small shop of her own.

Drink, poverty, and the pull of the neighbourhood bar undo those hopes step by step, in Zola's pitiless naturalist manner. The famous drinking scenes and the slow decay of Gervaise's household shocked readers and made the book a scandal and a success. It remains the great French novel of working-class Paris, powerful for its detail and its refusal to soften what it sees.
9952-the-faery-tales-of-weir:
Anna McClure Sholl's 1908 book gathers fairy tales of the town of Weir, a place readers can glimpse in the frontispiece, town after town like strings of pearls. The tales include the blue glove, the invisible wall, the tree in the dark wood, and the cat that winked.

Further stories tell of magic tears and the golden archer, each with its own small wonder and moral turn. Sholl writes in a gentle, old-fashioned manner suited to reading aloud. Children get enchantment without fright, and adults get a charming example of the literary fairy tale at its kindest.
absalom-s-hair:
Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson's Absalom's Hair opens on Harald Kaas at sixty, a giant gone to seed. His yacht no longer sails the coast in summer, and his club in Christiania sees him rarely. His herculean back is rounded, his teeth blackened by tobacco, and one little finger was bitten off by a man he had knocked down. He caresses the stump while his exploits grow.

Kaas lives at Hellebergene, a coastal estate his father, really a Kurt, reassembled by questionable means. His son Raf must inherit both the estate and its curse of violence. Bjørnson, Norway's national writer, tells a story of inherited temperament: strength curdling across generations. The title recalls the biblical Absalom, undone by pride. Raf's love and his father's shadow drive the short novel. It is among Bjørnson's darkest works, a saga compressed into a modern family tragedy.
ars-recte-vivendi-being-essays-contribut:
George William Curtis gathered Ars Recte Vivendi — the art of living rightly — from his 'Easy Chair' essays in Harper's Magazine. A preface explains that a college professor thought about a dozen of the essays covered the vital questions of hygiene, courtesy. morality well enough to make a book, and Curtis obliged with the collection.

The essays take up extravagance at college, brains and brawn, hazing, and secret societies, then theatre manners, woman's dress, tobacco in health and manners, duelling, and newspaper ethics. Each is short, urbane, and quietly argumentative, in the voice of a man of letters advising the republic on its everyday conduct. Together they form a Gilded Age manual of manners with a moral spine.
britannica-1911-abattoir: Abattoir is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry traces the word to the French verb abattre, to strike down. In English use it stands as a match for slaughter-house. That is, it names the place where animals meant for food are killed. The entry sends the reader onward to the slaughter-house article for the full account. Nothing further is stated in the notice itself, which serves as a cross-reference for the French term in the opening volume of the 1911 edition.
britannica-1911-aboukir:
Aboukir receives a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Egyptian village on the Mediterranean coast north-east of Alexandria holds a castle Mehemet Ali used as a state prison. Ruins of Egyptian, Greek, and Roman building crowd the shore.

Canopus's supposed site lies two miles south-east, by the dry Canopic Nile mouth. The bay eastward to Rosetta saw Nelson's battle of the Nile on the first of August 1798. A second Aboukir fight, French against Turks, followed in July 1799. Sir Ralph Abercromby's army landed here in March 1801 against entrenched French troops. One small coast village thus anchors three famous actions of the French wars.
britannica-1911-air:
Air, the atmosphere around the earth, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from an Indo-European root meaning breathe or blow. Greek writers set aer, the lower thick air, apart from aither, the upper pure air. For centuries air itself was taken for one single substance, the entry explains.

Pneumatic chemistry, the study of gases, broke that idea apart. Different airs were distinguished and renamed as gases: oxygen was dephlogisticated air, nitrogen was phlogisticated air, hydrogen was inflammable air, and carbonic acid gas was fixed air. The name air is now ordinarily kept for atmospheric air, the invisible elastic fluid we breathe, treated fully under Atmosphere. The entry also traces how air came to mean manner or appearance, and in music a melody.
britannica-1911-ardashir:
Ardashir is the modern form of the Persian royal name Artaxerxes, which means he whose empire is excellent. The 1911 Britannica article treats the three old kings of that name, then turns to Ardashir the First. He founded the new Persian, or Sassanian, empire. Greek and Roman writers tell little of him but his win over the Parthians and his wars with Rome. A sound tale of his rise comes from Persian sources kept by the Arab historian Tabari.

Ardashir was the second son of Papak, a king of Istakhr near the ruins of Persepolis. On the death of his father and elder brother, he made himself king, about the year 212. He slew his other brothers and warred on the small kings around him. The Parthian king Artabanus marched against him and fell in battle. Ardashir then took the title King of Kings of the Iranians.
britannica-1911-asir:
Asir is the subject of a district entry in the 1911 Britannica. Asir is a district in western Arabia. Hejaz, Nejd, and Yemen bound it on land sides. The Red Sea bounds it on the west side. Like Yemen it has two zones of land in form. One zone is a low strip along the coast. That strip runs twenty to thirty miles wide. The next zone is a tract of mountains inland.

Those hills fall steep on the west side face. They merge to a high plateau sloping north east. The low land is hot and bare of growth. Its chief port and two small ports are named. The hill tract stands high with a mild climate. Rain falls there on a steady round each year. Its vales are well watered and bear good crops. Grain and dates are the chief crops of those vales.
britannica-1911-bacharach-yair:
Bacharach, Yair (1639-1702), was a German rabbi and author of Hawwoth Yair, a collection of responsa, formal answers on Jewish law, besides other works. The short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry gives his dates, his chief book, and a judgment on his place in Jewish learning.

Bacharach was a man of wide culture, the entry says, and holds an honorable place among the pioneers of the Jewish Renaissance that opened toward the end of the 18th century. That later movement's forerunner is the whole claim made for him here: a rabbi whose learning reached beyond his own responsa toward a wider revival.
britannica-1911-back-choir: Back-Choir, also called the Retro-Choir, is the space behind the high altar in the choir of a church. In that space there is, or once was, a small altar standing back to back with the high altar itself. The short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry gives the name, its synonym, and this placing of a second, smaller altar directly behind the main one.
britannica-1911-baindir:
Baindir, the ancient Caystrus, is a town in Asiatic Turkey. It stands in the Aidin vilayet. The town sits in the valley of the Kuchuk Menderes river. Its people number under 10,000. Nearly half of them are Christian.

A branch of the Aidin railway links Baindir with Smyrna. That link supports its local trade. The town deals in cotton and figs. Raisins and tobacco also pass through it. River valley, railway, and four farm goods make the entry's whole account. It is one of the shortest town entries in this stretch of the encyclopedia.
britannica-1911-bartholomew-fair:
Bartholomew Fair, a fair held in West Smithfield, London, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as running from 1133 to 1855. Henry I granted its charter to Rahere, his former minstrel, who had taken holy orders and founded the priory of St Bartholomew nearby. The fair opened on St Bartholomew's Day, 24 August by the old calendar, and at first lasted a fortnight, though in 1691 it was cut to four days.

Ceremony and trade filled those days. The lord mayor of London opened the fair formally on its eve and stopped at Newgate to receive a cup of sack, a strong wine, from the governor. By 1641 the fair sprawled across four parishes. Above all it was a vast national market and the chief cloth sale in the kingdom, where the Merchant Taylors' silver yard measure tested the cloth sellers' measures. It closed for good in 1855.
britannica-1911-bath-chair:
Bath-chair is the name of a small wheeled vehicle described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It has a folding hood, which can be used open or closed, and a glass front to shield the person seated inside. The chair is mounted on three or four wheels. It is drawn or pushed by hand. Its user was moved by an attendant, not riding at speed, which fixes its use for the sick and frail.

A stronger form could take animal power. If a donkey or small pony had to draw it, the chair sat on four wheels instead. It then had turning gear, so the front wheels could steer, as on a small carriage. The entry names the maker of the first such chair: James Heath, of the city of Bath, who worked a little before the middle of the 1700s. The vehicle took its name from that city.
britannica-1911-beaumanoir:
Beaumanoir is a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of a lordship in Brittany in France and the famed house that took its name. One lord of that house led Breton knights in a war for the duchy. Two claimants fought for the duchy, backed by the kings of France and England.

The heart of the entry is a set fight of thirty men on each side. The clash came after raids broke a truce in the district. Swords, daggers, and axes made the fight long and grim. A famed cry told the hurt Breton chief to drink his blood for thirst. A late charge on horseback won the day for the Breton side.
britannica-1911-bikanir:
Bikanir is a native state of India in the Rajputana agency, covering 23,311 square miles. The 1911 Britannica article paints it as a desolate tract of sand. No stream runs through it all year. Sand hills rise 20 to 100 feet, so loose that travellers sink as in snow. Two streams, the Katli and Ghaggar, die in its sands. Wells must be dug 250 to 340 feet deep for water.

The people live mainly by pasturage, the article says. Camels are their chief stock, and their horses fetch good prices. Sheep wool gives them cloth and good blankets. Leather work, sugar refining, ivory carving, and metal work fill out the trades. Salt crusts from dried rain lakes serve homes and trade. The article ends with the reigning maharaja's services. His Bikanir Camel Corps fought in China in 1901 and Somaliland in 1904.
britannica-1911-cantemir:
Cantemir is the name of a famed family of Tatar origin, treated in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The family came from the Crimea in the sixteen hundreds and settled in Moldavia. Constantine Cantemir became prince of Moldavia in sixteen eighty five. He ruled till sixteen ninety three.

He was a good and careful ruler, the entry says. He shielded the folk from greedy tax men and brought peace to his land. His son Antioch ruled twice after him. Constantine's youngest brother Demetrius became prince in seventeen ten. He ruled one year, then joined Peter the Great against the Turks. Beaten, he moved to Russia with his family and died there. He was famed as one of the greatest linguists of his time, with eleven languages.
britannica-1911-carrick-on-suir:
Carrick-on-Suir is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town of County Tipperary, Ireland, on the north bank of the Suir. Its urban district held 5406 people in 1901. The town was once walled and keeps old buildings, among them a castle raised in 1309 that was a seat of the dukes of Ormonde and still belongs to the Butler family. Across the river stands the suburb of Carrickbeg, in County Waterford, where an abbey was founded in 1336.

A bridge of the fourteenth century and a newer one join the two banks. The woollen trade that once made the town famous is gone, but a strong export trade in farm produce continues. Condensed milk is made in the town, slate is quarried nearby, and some coal leaves from the neighbouring fields. Dredging has improved the river channel, which is tidal up to the town and lined with quays.
britannica-1911-chair:
Chair, the common seat for one person, is traced from the old world in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word runs back through French to the Latin cathedra, a seat. For most of its long life the chair was no common thing. It was a mark of state and rank, kept for the great.

Not till the sixteenth century did chairs grow common in homes. Chest, bench, and stool served plain folk till then. What we know of old chairs comes from carved stone, paint, and tomb finds. Egypt made chairs of ebony and ivory, with legs shaped as the legs of beasts. Nineveh shows backless chairs with legs that end in claws or hoofs. The word the chair still names the seat of rule at public meets.
britannica-1911-choir:
Choir, the singers and their place, is opened in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word came through French from the Latin chorus. Men spelled it quire till the late seventeenth century in England. A choir is the body that sings the music of a church rite. It is also the part of the church set aside for them.

In English great churches the choir holds men and boys. They split into two sets on the north and south sides. Those sides take their names from the dean and the precentor. White surplices mark the singers in such churches by old custom. Parish churches took up that dress from the mid last century. Rome sets its singers in a loft, less in the eye.
britannica-1911-coir: Coir is a rough, strong fibre. It is taken from the outer husk of the coconut. Its name comes from a Malay word for cord. That word is tied to a verb that means to be twisted. The hosted entry is a single short statement of that origin and source. It gives no account of how the fibre is worked or used. It points the reader to the entry on the coconut palm for more.
britannica-1911-elzevir:
Elzevir is the name of a famed family of Dutch printers of the 17th century. The family came first from Louvain, where Louis, who made the name famous, was born in 1540. Trained as a bookbinder, he left his home country in 1580 for his Protestant faith and settled in Leiden as bookbinder and bookseller.

Of Louis's five sons, Bonaventure, born in 1583, is the most celebrated, and in 1626 he took his nephew Abraham into partnership. The fame of the Elzevir editions rests chiefly on that firm's work. Their Greek and Hebrew printing is judged weaker than that of the Aldi and the Estiennes. Their small editions, though, in 12mo, 16mo, and 24mo, cannot be beaten for neat design, clear type, and fine paper. The entry names their Greek New Testaments of 1624 and 1633 and their Petites Républiques series of French works on history and politics.
britannica-1911-fair:
Fair, in the words of Lord Coke quoted by the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, is a greater kind of market that comes back at longer gaps. Fairs, markets, and marts are all gatherings of buyers and sellers at a set place, ruled by law or custom. In England no fair can exist in law without a franchise from the crown, Parliament, or long use.

Set trading days grew from the hardship and danger of travel in early times. Crowds drawn for worship, war, or law courts gave trade its chance, as at the festivals of Delos and the Olympic games. Fairs cling closest to church feasts, and the word is traced to the Latin feria, a festival day. Most great medieval fairs were grants to abbots and bishops, who took their tolls. The link still shows in the German word Messen and the Breton kirmess, church mass.
britannica-1911-fakir:
Fakir is an article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from an Arabic term for poor, and first meant a Muslim religious beggar. By the time of the article it was used chiefly for Hindu holy men and wanderers in India. The entry sorts Indian fakirs into two broad classes.

The first class is the religious orders. Their members live in monasteries that serve as centres of teaching and poor relief. The second class is wandering beggars who live off alms and the fears of villagers. The article describes the harsh acts some perform, holding arms aloft until the muscles waste. It is a period account, written in the blunt tone of its day, and it cites Oman's study of Indian saints and the census reports.
britannica-1911-fir:
Fir is a name first given to the Scotch pine, explains a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Now it is often used as a broad term for the true conifers. In a stricter sense it belongs to the spruces and the silver firs. Those are two genera in modern botany.

Firs differ from pines and larches in their leaves. Their needle leaves sit singly on the shoots, not in clusters from a sheath. Their cones are made of thin round scales laid close over each other. The trees most often have a straight trunk and a cone like shape. Each year a ring of branches grows out from the lead shoot. In spruces the cones hang down when ripe. In silver firs the cones stand upright and their scales fall when the seed ripens.
britannica-1911-friedmann-meir: Meir Friedmann (1831-1908) was a Hungarian Jewish scholar whose editions of the Midrash are the standard texts. His chief editions were the Sifre in 1864, the Mekhilta in 1870, and the Pesiqla Rabbathi in 1880, and at his death he was editing the Sifra. Though full of regard for tradition, Friedmann handled the Rabbinic texts by modern scientific methods. The entry credits him with notable service to the critical study of the Midrash and to the history of early homilies. It is a very short notice.
britannica-1911-glair:
Glair, in the 1911 Britannica, is the white of an egg. The word comes from the French glaire, probably from the Latin clarus, clear or bright. From that first sense, the entry moves to a made preparation of egg white used in the crafts.

In bookbinding and in gilding, glair serves two ends: it helps retain the gold, and it acts as a varnish. The adjective glairy is then defined for substances that share egg white's nature. They are viscous, see-through and sticky to the touch. The notice is a brief word entry, giving origin, the raw substance, its workshop use, and the adjective formed from it.
britannica-1911-hair:
Hair is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the coat that grows on mammals. The word is shared across the Teutonic tongues. Hair is an outgrowth of the outer skin, the epidermis. The term is used by likeness for threads on insects and plants. It can even name things that merely look like hair. For the build of animal hair, the text points to other entries. Those cover skin, fur, and leather in more depth.

The part shown here deals with hair and mankind. Human hair holds a key place in the study of race. Its length, form, and colour vary by group. Its thickness and its look under a lens vary as well. Those traits tend to persist across long spans of time. That persistence gave hair its weight in the science of man. The entry shows how a plain trait became a measure in that field.
britannica-1911-hawawir:
The Hawawir are an African tribe of Semitic origin. They dwell in the Bayuda desert of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. Their range follows the road from Debba toward Khartum. It runs from Ambigol to Wadi Bishāra. They have adopted none of the negro customs around them. Cheek-gashing and elaborate hairdressing are both rejected. Large herds of oxen form their wealth. Sheep and camels complete those herds.

The entry is one of the shortest tribal notices in its band. It fixes the tribe's origin, desert and range. It notes what customs they refuse from neighbours. It ends with their livestock, their main resource. No numbers, chiefs or history are given. The notice stands as a bare location-and-livelihood record.
britannica-1911-heir:
Heir, in law, is one who succeeds by descent to an estate of inheritance. Latin heres lies behind the word. A root meaning to grasp is proposed for it. The technical sense contrasts with next of kin. Next of kin succeed to personal property instead. General usage now covers anyone entitled to inherit property or titles. Rules of descent themselves sit under Inheritance and Succession.

Several kinds of heir are then distinguished. An heir apparent's right is indefeasible if he outlives the ancestor. An heir presumptive can be displaced by a nearer birth. A customary heir inherits by local custom, as in borough-English. There the youngest son takes the property. Gavelkind instead makes all sons joint heirs. An heir general is the ordinary heir at law. An ultimate heir takes by escheat when proper heirs fail. Scots law widens the term to personal property too.
britannica-1911-kashmir:
Kashmir, or Cashmere, is a native state of India taking in much of the Himalayan system north of the Punjab. Its segment sits in a hosted file shared with Kashgar and Kashmiri material. The land is famed in song for its beauty, as in Moore's Lalla Rookh, and it is the chief health resort for Europeans in India. In rule it guards one of the ways into India on the northwest frontier.

The state's proper name is Jammu and Kashmir. It covers an area put at 80,900 square miles, with 2,905,578 people in 1901, a rise of over 14 per cent in ten years. Tibet bounds it on the east, the Punjab and the North West Frontier on the south and west. It stands under the Government of India, which is present through a resident. Its lands count Jammu, Kashmir, Ladakh, Baltistan, and Gilgit.
britannica-1911-kirriemuir:
Kirriemuir is a police burgh of Forfarshire, Scotland, with 4096 people in 1901. It stands on a height above the glen of the Gairie. Forfar lies six and a quarter miles southeast by a branch line of the Caledonian railway, of which Kirriemuir is the terminus. It has libraries, a public hall, and a park. Its staple industry is linen weaving.

The hand loom held on here longer than in any other place in Scotland, and it is not yet wholly gone. The Reverend Dr Alexander Whyte and J. M. Barrie are natives of the town. Barrie made it famous under the name of Thrums. The original Secession church, the kirk of the Auld Lichts, was founded in 1806 and rebuilt in 1893. Kinnordy, eleven and a half miles northwest, was the birthplace of Sir Charles Lyell the geologist. Cortachy castle, about 4 miles north, is the seat of the earl of Airlie.
britannica-1911-meir:
Meïr, a Jewish rabbi of the second century, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Asia Minor, and legend makes him a descendant of Nero's house. He was the most notable disciple of the teacher Aqiba. After the Hadrianic repressions of the year 135, he helped refound the schools at Usha.

His wife Beruriah is often cited in the Talmud for her faith and generosity. She was a daughter of a martyr of the persecution. The article retells her famed answer on the death of their two sons. She first asked her husband whether a treasure left in trust must be returned. He said it must, and she led him to the children's bodies. Then she quoted Job: the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. Meïr's devotion to a teacher who had lapsed from the faith is also praised.
britannica-1911-mohair:
Mohair is the hair of the Angora goat, a breed first kept in the parts of Asiatic Turkey around Angora. The 1911 Britannica article traces the word to an Arabic term that meant choice or select. It was used first for cloth made of goat hair. In the seventeenth century the English form was bent by its likeness to the word hair. The French took the word back as moire, for a watered silk cloth.

A good mohair fibre runs seven to eight inches long and shines with a bright gloss. It feels soft and springy, and its colour is most often a clear white. The scales on its shaft are faint, unlike the full scales of wool, and the fibre is solid through. Fleeces vary a great deal by district. The trade at Constantinople sorts many grades, from poor Van mohair up to the finest type.
britannica-1911-montclair:
Montclair is a town in Essex county, New Jersey, north west of Newark. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits at the base and on the slopes of the Orange Mountains. Two rail lines and electric lines link it with near cities and towns.

Montclair serves as a home suburb for New York and near cities. Its schools are praised, and it holds a hospital and a public library. A state normal school and Montclair academy add to its school life. The lower town was settled in about sixteen seventy five as Cranetown. It took the name Montclair in eighteen sixty eight and town rank in eighteen ninety four.
britannica-1911-pulaski-casimir:
Pulaski, Casimir is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Polish count and soldier. Born in Podolia in 1748, Pulaski took a leading share under his father, Count Joseph Pulaski, in forming the confederation of Bar and in the fighting that followed. He rose to command the Polish patriot forces. Driven into exile about 1772, he went to America and joined the army of Washington in 1777.

The article follows his American service in detail. He made his mark at once at Brandywine. He fought at Germantown, raised a mixed corps called the Pulaski legion, and defended Charleston in May 1779. He was mortally wounded in the failed attack on Savannah on the ninth of October and died two days later on board ship.
britannica-1911-rabah-zobeir:
Rabah Zobeir, who died in 1900 after conquering Bornu by Lake Chad, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bornu was an old sultanate on the west shore of the lake. Rabah began as a slave or follower of Zobeir Pasha. In 1879 he held command of Zobeir forces in the Bahr-el-Ghazal with Suleiman.

After defeat by Gessi Pasha, Rabah fled west with some seven hundred black slave soldiers. He made himself master of Kreich and Dar Banda. Arms seized from a French party in 1891, among them 300 rifles, sped his march. He settled in Bagirmi and in 1893 overthrew the sultan of Bornu. The entry grants that he ruled the land with real skill.
britannica-1911-romesh-chandra-mitra-sir:
Romesh Chandra Mitra is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an Indian judge. Born in 1840, he rose as the new high courts took shape in India. The entry first traces the men who held the Calcutta bench before him. One of them, Dwarka Nath Mitra, is praised as a judge of rare gifts.

On the death of Anukul Chandra Mukerji in 1871, Romesh took his seat. He kept up the high name of those who went before him. For near twenty years, down to 1890, he did his work with credit. In 1882 the viceroy, Lord Ripon, had him act as chief justice. That post was the top judge post in the Indian empire.
britannica-1911-sayyid-ahmad-khan-sir:
Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan (1817-1898) was a Muslim educationist and reformer in India, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives his work. He was born at Delhi, of a family that had come with the Muslim conquest and held high posts under the Mogul emperors. His weak English kept him from rising above a small cause court judgeship. Yet he earned the standing of the acknowledged leader of his community.

To the British he gave loyal service, and when the mutiny reached Bijnor in 1857 the British residents there owed their lives to his courage and tact. His hold on his own faith was firm, and in 1876 he defended Islam in essays written in London. He used his standing to act as interpreter between Muslims and their rulers.
britannica-1911-sedan-chair:
Sedan chair is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a chair for one that men carry from place to place. It is a shut box with panes at the sides. A door at the front swings on a hinge for the man to step in. The roof can be swung up so he can stand as he steps out. Two men bear it on poles.

In Paris and in London the chair man was a set part of street life. In one town he was most times a man of one French tract. In the other he was most times an Irish man. The chair was a smart way to move in towns till about a span of years past the date of the book.
britannica-1911-sir:
Sir is a title of honor, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its use and its roots. The word comes through French forms from the Latin senior, the comparative of senex, meaning old. In British lands the title is now kept for baronets, knights of the orders, and knights bachelor.

The entry stresses a key rule of use: Sir goes before the first name only, never with the surname alone, as in Sir William Jones. In older days the word was used loosely for any man of rank, much like lord. Selden is cited to show that its fixed use with the names of knights is itself very old.
britannica-1911-tapir:
The tapir is the subject of an animal entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tapirs are an old group of hoofed mammals with odd numbers of toes. They keep many traits of the early hoofed beasts of long past ages. The entry says they have changed but little over vast spans of time.

Their fore feet have four toes set in hoofs, with a large pad beneath. They are massive in build, with short stout limbs and a long head. The nose and upper lip stretch out to form a short flexible trunk. The entry uses build and feet to place tapirs among their hoofed kin.
castles-in-the-air:
Baroness Emmuska Orczy lets Hector Ratichon tell his own story. He is a Paris police agent at 96 Rue Daunou. He boasts of serving Robespierre, then Napoleon, then King Louis. Yet twenty years of zeal left him poor. His fat, devoted assistant Theodore, and a run of clients high and low, complete his little office world.

Linked tales follow Ratichon's schemes against thieves, blackmailers, and conspirators, each scheme promising the fortune that always slips away. He narrates with huge self-regard, blind to how often luck, or others, save him. Orczy plays the memoirs for comedy and suspense at once, in a Paris still shaking from revolution, empire, and restoration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arthur-marie-:
Arthur Marie Le Hir, biblical scholar and Orientalist, was born at Morlaix in Finistère, in the Quimper diocese, on 5 December 1811 and died at Paris on 13 January 1868. Entering St. Sulpice seminary in Paris in 1833, he entered the Sulpicians after ordination and became professor of theology, then professor of Sacred Scripture and Hebrew. He had been formed by Garnier, whom Renan called a scholar with solid knowledge of languages and the fullest knowledge of exegesis, or biblical interpretation, of any Catholic in France.

Le Hir taught those subjects until his death some thirty years later. Through his own labour and that of his student Renan he powerfully influenced the revival of biblical and Oriental scholarship in France. Renan judged him France's best Hebrew and Syriac scholar in his generation, thoroughly versed in biblical science, including current German works, whose theories he exposed and strongly combated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benadir:
Benadir is a short geographical and mission entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, covering the Prefecture Apostolic in Italian Somaliland. Its bounds run along the East African coast from the Gulf of Aden to the Juba river, an area the entry puts at nearly twice the size of Italy. The Indian Ocean forms its eastern edge.

Mission history fills the second half, with the commercial company that first held the coast giving way to direct Italian rule. Catholic missionaries, schools, and stations appear as a small presence in a largely Muslim land. The entry reads as a map, a boundary list, and a brief mission report in one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-o-bruad:
A biographical entry presents David O'Bruadair, an Irish poet born about 1625, probably in Barrymore, County Cork, and dead in January 1698. Well schooled in Irish, Latin, and English, he shows the influence of Geoffrey Keating, his favourite Irish author. His elegies mourn great Munster families, above all the Bourkes, Fitzgeralds, and Barrys who later befriended him in poverty.

All his poems, historical, social, or elegiac, carry a freshness unusual for the seventeenth century and preserve details of contemporary life and manners. Two epithalamia, wedding poems rare in Irish letters, celebrate the marriages of Una and Eleanore Bourke. His satires bite against Cromwellian planters and Ormonde's flatterers, while his religious poems, above all on the Passion, show great beauty and depth of feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-despair:
A moral theology entry on despair, the voluntary and complete giving up of all hope of saving one's soul. It is no passive mood: will and intellect join in deciding that salvation is impossible. Motives vary, from sins judged too great for pardon to human nature judged too weak for grace, or God judged unwilling to help.

Mere dread of the future is not despair, and neither is the fearful shrinking of the faint-hearted, who still trusts while trembling at personal faults. Despair may also carry heresy when it assents to a claim against faith, such as God refusing needful aid. Counted always a mortal sin, it shuts off escape and often leaves its victims to surrender to every indulgence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-burckmai:
Augsburg painter Hans Burckmair, born in 1473 to the painter Thomas Burckmair, learned first from his father, then from Schongauer in Alsace, and afterwards in Italy. With the elder Holbein he painted seven great Roman churches on panels for St. Catherine's monastery between 1501 and 1504, taking St. Peter's, the Lateran, and Santa Croce for his own.

Later panels include a Crucifixion of 1519, St. John on Patmos and Esther before Ahasuerus of 1528, and a self-portrait with his wife of 1529 in which she holds a mirror showing two skulls. For Emperor Maximilian he cut hundreds of woodblocks for the Austrian Saints, Teuerdank, Triumph, Weisskunig, and Genealogy, moving German art from Gothic gold grounds toward Renaissance colour and landscape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kafiristan-an:
Kafiristan and Kashmir was a prefecture created by Leo XIII in 1887 in India's extreme north. Before that year the district belonged to the Capuchin Diocese of Lahore. It was then entrusted to the Mill Hill Fathers of the English Foreign Missions. The prefecture covered important British military stations, including Peshawur by the Khyber Pass, Nowshera, and Rawalpindi, headquarters of the Northern Army.

Rawalpindi was also the residence of the Prefect Apostolic, Dominic Wagner, nominated in 1900. Convents at Murree and Rawalpindi ran boarding schools, a military orphanage, and day schools; a hospital for native women and children was planned under Dr. Elizabeth Bielby. At Baramulla in Kashmir, Father Simon and twelve lay teachers taught three hundred native boys. Of some fifteen million inhabitants, about five thousand were Catholics, against twelve and a half million Mohammedans, two million Hindus, and half a million Buddhists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ophir:
Ophir, in the Bible, names both a people and a gold country reached by Solomon's fleet. The people appear among Jectan's sons dwelling from Messa toward Sephar in the east, while the place sent gold, silver, sandalwood, precious stones, ivory, apes, and peacocks to Ezion-Geber.

Its site stays unknown. The Bible gives no position, only a three-year round voyage, and scholars weigh products, gold passages, and trade routes to place it in Arabia, India, or Africa. The entry judges each identification on its evidence. Gold passages in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah mark it as a gold-producing region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-iv-the:
Philip IV, called the Fair, was king of France from 1285 to 1314, son of Philip III and Isabel of Aragon. Born at Fontainebleau in 1268 and crowned at Reims with his wife Jeanne of Navarre, he joined Navarre, Champagne, and Brie to the royal domain. He took Viviers and Lyons from the empire, seized La Marche and Angoumois, and occupied nearly all Guienne against Edward I before returning it as his daughter Isabel's dower.

Against Flanders he suffered defeat at Courtrai, then avenged it at Zierikzee and Mons-en-Puelle, keeping Lille, Douai, Orchies, and Valenciennes by 1305. With legists like Enguerrand de Marigny he centralized government and imposed a rigorous fiscal system. His reign's other great thread ran through his quarrels with Boniface VIII and his dealings with Clement V over the Templars. He died at Fontainebleau in 1314.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rusaddir:
Rusaddir is a titular see of Mauritania Tingitana, a Phoenician settlement whose name signifies a lofty cape. Ptolemy and Pliny call it town and port, and the Antonine Itinerary also mentions it. In the Middle Ages it was the Berber city of Mlila, now Melilla. In 1497 it fell to the Duke of Medina Sidonia, returning to Spain's crown in 1506.

Since then famines and sieges fill its history, most renowned that of 1774. In 1909 it was the seat of warfare between Spain and the Rif tribes. Melilla, after Ceuta the most important Spanish fortress on the African coast, has about 9,000 inhabitants. It is built on the east slope of a steep rock 1,640 feet high, with the Fort of Rosario. A free port since 1881, it trades with the Rif. No bishop of this see is recorded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sandomir:
Sandomir, Polish Sandomierz, is a very ancient Polish city still showing prehistoric building traces. Its 6,891 people included 2,364 Catholics, 46 Orthodox, and 3,433 Jews. When Mieszko I brought Christianity to Poland in the tenth century, he built churches there to St Nicholas and St John. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia makes the city a gallery of holy figures.

In the Middle Ages Sandomir grew into a centre of political and religious life. Blessed Salome, daughter of Leszek the Fair and wife of Hungary's Koloman, lived there. So did Blessed Adelaide, daughter of Casimir the Just, who founded St John's parish church and was buried there in 1211. Blessed Vincent Kadlubek, canonised after a fruitful ministry, lived there too. The Dominican Czeslaw, brother of Hyacinth, and Hyacinth himself complete the roll.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sistine-choir:
The Sistine Choir descends from the papal schola cantorum, a company of singers under Sylvester I in 314 to 335. The word schola then meant a guild of equals in a calling, not a school, and that guild character clung to the choir. Hilary II ordered the pontifical singers to live in community. Gregory the Great fixed the Lateran institution and added a second at Saint Peter's, which served as a preparatory school for the first.

After the papal move to Avignon, Clement V formed a new choir of French singers favouring new music. Sixtus IV fixed the choir at twenty-four singers by bull in November 1483, six for each part, and the body became the capella sistina. Julius II founded the capella Julia in 1512 as a nursery for the Sistine Choir. Leo X, a musician, made a musician its head, turning virtuosi on equal footing into a vocal body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-casimir:
St. Casimir was prince of Poland, born in the royal palace at Cracow on 3 October 1458. He died at the court of Grodno on 4 March 1484. This entry follows the grandson of Wladislaus II Jagiello, king of Poland, who brought Christianity to Lithuania. He was King Casimir IV and Queen Elizabeth's second son; Elizabeth was an Austrian princess, daughter of Albert II, emperor of Germany and king of Bohemia and Hungary.

His uncle Wladislaus III, king of Poland and Hungary, died at Varna in 1444 defending Christianity against the Turks. His elder brother Wladislaus took Bohemia's throne in 1471 and Hungary's in 1490. Four younger brothers, John I, Albert, Alexander, and Sigismund, in turn held the Polish throne. The youngest, Frederick, became archbishop of Gnesen, bishop of Cracow, and cardinal in 1493. The young princes' early training was entrusted to Father Dlugosz, the Polish historian.
charles-lamb-a-memoir:
Charles Lamb: A Memoir, by Barry Cornwall, records the essayist Lamb from the memory of one of his last surviving friends. Cornwall was the pen name of Bryan Waller Procter, who writes in May 1866, in his seventy seventh year. He believes himself nearly the only man left who knew Elia intimately. He knew him best in Lamb's final seventeen years or so. He is proud to attach his name to his friend's.

The memoir proceeds by recollection rather than record. A biography of Lamb holds few events. One devotion predominates: the care of his sister Mary, whose madness shadowed both their lives. Anecdotes of the India House clerk who wrote the Essays of Elia, his talk, his jokes, and his tenderness fill the pages. A new generation, Cornwall hopes, will extend its sympathy to a humorist he counts among England's rarest and most delicate.
child-christopher-and-goldilind-the-fair:
William Morris wrote Child Christopher and Goldilind the Fair, published in 1895, one of his late prose romances set in an imagined medieval world. Christopher is the young son of the King of Oakenrealm, stolen as a child and raised as a thrall in a forest house, with no knowledge of his birth. Goldilind is a king's daughter kept a near prisoner by a countess who envies her beauty.

Their paths cross, and the tale follows flight, disguise, battles, and a long road back to rightful rule. Morris tells it in rich, archaic prose thick with woodland, hall, and sea. The romances he wrote in his last years helped found the modern fantasy tale, and this one shows his craft at its ripest.
doe-osti-17076581-insertion-readiness-fo:
Stephen Taller and six Oak Ridge colleagues report in September 2026 on getting an Alloy 709 irradiation campaign ready to insert into a reactor. Alloy 709 is a strong steel favored for hot advanced reactor parts, and it is working through code qualification. Radiation effects, though, are missing from that data set, so test capsules must gather them.

The report gives a status update on capsules bound for the High Flux Isotope Reactor and details the design of a creep capsule. Such a capsule holds samples under steady load while they are irradiated, so creep under radiation can be measured. Precipitates inside the alloy pin dislocations and give it better creep strength than standard stainless grades.
doe-osti-3015786-advancing-a-low-tempera:
Holocene Climate Corporation's final report for award DE-FE0032269, written by Tobias Rueesch and Anca Timofte in November 2025, covers bench-scale tests of a direct air capture process. The process pulls carbon dioxide straight from the air. It uses amino acids and guanidine compounds, a chemistry first developed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and licensed to Holocene.

The goals were to cut the heat needed to release captured carbon dioxide, and to shape the air contactor so air passes through with less pressure drop. Work included long-term sorbent stability tests and plans to make about one kilogram of the guanidine sorbent. That sorbent production milestone was not finished, because the project ended early. The report supports the Energy Department goal of removing carbon for under 100 dollars per net tonne by 2031.
doe-osti-3028687-mechanical-property-mea:
David Hoelzer, Caleb Massey, Jesse Werden, and Thak Sang Byun of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, with Stuart Maloy of Pacific Northwest and Annabelle Le Coq. They measured mechanical properties of reactor steels irradiated in the High Flux Isotope Reactor, in ORNL/TM-2025/4017, dated July 2025. The alloys are ferritic-martensitic steels and oxide dispersion strengthened steels, the two families proposed for hard nuclear duty. Strength and ductility after irradiation are the licensing facts that matter.

Tensile results are compared at fixed dose across alloys with names like 14YWT, 9YWTV, OFRAC, and two HT9 variants. For 14YWT-SM13, flow stress behavior looked similar at doses of 8 and 16 displacements per atom and at test temperatures of 385 and 525 degrees. Across the set, rising dose generally pushed strength up and ductility down, the standard radiation hardening story the data are there to quantify.
doe-osti-3366753-reimagining-heating-ven:
Slipstream's June 2026 Building America report, by Shannon Stendel, Scott Pigg, Brady Peeks, and partners at the Florida Solar Energy Center, rethinks heating and cooling for new manufactured homes. Manufactured housing is America's unsubsidized affordable stock, yet it often ships with crude HVAC. The DOE-funded project asked which innovations offer the best mix of energy performance and industry uptake.

Field trials included heat pumps in Oregon and Florida homes, with weeks of auxiliary resistance-only operation in Oregon for comparison against the pump. A plug-and-play refrigeration connection was explored so factory or service technicians could swap heat pump components without handling refrigerant on site. Guidance for manufacturers closes the report, aimed at adoption rather than demonstration alone. Results are stated to differ from standard rating conditions by design.
doe-osti-3374045-hsr-lattice-model-in-th:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229823-2026-TECH, dated May 2026, by G. Robert-Demolaize with J. Scott Berg, documents a lattice model for the Hadron Storage Ring of the Electron-Ion Collider. The model follows the hadron beam direction and adds high-order field harmonics of the dipole magnets, the small field errors that bend beams off their ideal path. It updates the baseline release named 250730a.

The note explains how the harmonics were folded into the model without rewriting each bending magnet. Both the MAD-X/Xsuite and Bmad code versions amend each magnet with a body gradient in place of an integrated value. A second half covers how the magnets were actually installed in the old RHIC tunnel, since a magnet's position and facing matter as much as its field. Installation conventions are taken from the RHIC Configuration Manual, keyed to the clockwise Blue ring.
doe-osti-3488006-analyses-of-cumulus-mix: Final report on award DE-SC0022887, by Zhiming Kuang, analyzes cumulus cloud mixing with aircraft data and large-eddy simulations. Aircraft cloud data are costly and underused, the author notes. A classic chart method, the Paluch diagram, had been doubted since a 2008 study. The project traced the doubt to a fixable bias source. Paluch results had been compared against particle tracking treated as truth. Large-domain simulations then mimicked field campaigns to test fixes.
doe-osti-3682459-initial-testing-of-the-:
Oak Ridge field notes, dated August 2026, record first tests of a portable long-wave spectrometer, the D&P 102 FTIR. David Hughes ran the sensor, Shannon Meade coordinated samples, and Abbie Faxon logged data. The goal was to gather upwelling and downwelling radiance spectra. From those, the team can work out emissivity and apparent temperature. A second goal was to prove the new instrument works.

Sites were the east patio of building 5800 and the firefighter training ground. Targets ran from hot and cold blackbodies to shrubs, play sand, tarps, bubble wrap, concrete, and packing foam. A second outing targeted spots where PFAS had or had not been deposited in the past. Bulk PFAS in buckets could not be opened, so those shots were missed. Phone photos and a borrowed GPS unit logged each spot.
doe-osti-3683895-resstock-measure-docume:
Three ResStock upgrade measures for homes are documented in National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5500-99818, dated September 2026. Jes Brossman and Philip White are the printed authors. ResStock models the United States housing stock to test energy upgrades at scale. The three measures here are light air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing with insulation. All three apply at once in the model, and their order does not change the outputs.

Target levels are spelled out for each measure. Ducts in fitting homes are sealed to at most five percent leakage to the outside and wrapped to a set insulation level. Attic floors rise to one insulation grade in the warmest climate zone and a higher grade in zones two through eight. Results give a single building example first. Stock-wide energy and bill effects follow. A companion set of papers holds the deeper modelling assumptions.
doe-osti-3874839-final-report-on-aluminu:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-28313, issued September 16, 2026, reviews who should supply the lab's aluminum 4047 filler wire. Robert Madigan, Michael McAninch, and Joris Hochanadel are the printed authors. The lab wants a maker with full control of the process, from ingot to packaged spool. It also wants small off-the-shelf buys, so stock stays fresh. Seven sellers were contacted and scored against a shared criteria table.

Only Lincoln Electric controls every step, smelting through packaging, at its Ontario, Canada plant. Hobart and AlcoTec buy starting rod but specify tighter chemistry than the welding standard allows, then draw and package the wire themselves. The other four firms mainly re-sell wire made elsewhere. The alloy is prone to porosity from surface hydrogen, so heated, dry storage is advised. The report recommends trial spools from several heats, hydrogen checks, and weld tests before any contract.
elsie-at-the-world-s-fair:
Martha Finley takes her clan to Chicago in Elsie at the World's Fair, from Dodd, Mead and Company in 1894. A note thanks the Chicago Record's history of the fair and two art series for the descriptions and statistics of the White City and its exhibits. The tale opens not at the fair but at a wedding.

Hugh Lilburn presses his betrothed Ella for a speedy marriage, since her brother has carried off the cousin who kept his house. Sisters come up from the far South, parties follow, and no bridal trip is taken. Kin then travel north and west by steamer and rail toward the fair. On deck, a tired daughter begs to rest in a steamer chair and listen to the talk, and her father sets her bedtime like a child. Finley mixes family romance with a guided tour of the great fair of 1893.
georges-guynemer-knight-of-the-air:
Henry Bordeaux tells the life of Georges Guynemer, France's famed fighter pilot of the First World War, in a book translated by Louise Morgan Sill and published in 1918. Theodore Roosevelt wrote the introduction. The book is shaped as three cantos: Childhood, Launched into Space, and At the Zenith. Guynemer's frail health as a boy makes his rise the more striking.

Bordeaux follows him from his first victory through the Aisne, Verdun, and the Somme in 1916 and into 1917. One scene shows the wounded pilot, fallen from the sky, walking before the troops as they sing the Marseillaise. The tone is heroic and tender. French readers took Guynemer as a knight of the air, and this book, written while the war still raged, shows why.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIABirdAir_CIA_:
Bird Air was a small airline in Southeast Asia with a long shadow: it grew out of Bird and Sons, a company that flew for the CIA in Laos. Ralph Blumenthal's article, The Mysterious Airlift, follows that airline's strange career.

Proprietary airlines let the agency move men and cargo under commercial cover, and Bird Air's operations sat inside that system during the secret war years. Blumenthal, a New York Times reporter, traces the company through its contracts and questions. The article preserves investigative reporting on the CIA's air arm, where the paperwork was meant to say as little as possible.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAGeorgeClair_:
Clair George ran the CIA's clandestine service as deputy director for operations, and his secret life ended in a courtroom: he was convicted in the Iran-Contra affair. Benjamin Weiser's Washington Post Magazine cover story of May 17, 1992, profiles him at that fall.

Weiser traces George's career through the agency's covert wars to the arms-for-hostages scandal that put his generation of spymasters on trial. The piece is a cover-story portrait: the charming operations chief as a man of the old CIA, overtaken by its exposure. It is preserved complete for readers of intelligence history.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OswaldAffairLeo:
Gaeton Fonzi reviewed Leo Sauvage's 'The Oswald Affair' for Book Week on October 23, 1966. The review ran under the title 'Burning Questions.' Sauvage, a French journalist, had written one of the first books to dispute the Warren Report. Fonzi examines the contradictions and omissions he found in the official account.

Fonzi later became an investigator for Congress on the same case, which gives his early review a second life. Here, in 1966, he is a reviewer measuring a Frenchman's doubts against the American record. The review marks the moment the Warren Report's critics moved from pamphlets into the book pages of national newspapers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH:
Charles Horman and Frank Teruggi were Americans living in Chile when the 1973 coup struck. Both were killed by the military regime. Chile in Their Hearts presents a briefing book built around a new book on their murders.

Their cases became famous through the film Missing and through their families' long search for the truth. The briefing book returns to the documents: what American officials knew, and when they knew it. For readers, the collection joins the personal story of two young men to the paper record of a government that failed to protect them.
l-assommoir:
Émile Zola's novel L'Assommoir is read here in English, in thirteen chapters. It opens with Gervaise, who has waited up until two in the morning for Lantier. She throws herself across the bed, feverish and in tears.

Gervaise, Lantier, and their children eat at a cheap place called the Two-Headed Calf. Lantier stays out late night after night, offering thin excuses. Zola builds the story from such plain, hard details of working life. The novel shows poverty and drink pressing on a Paris family. The title names a cheap drinking shop central to the tale. Work, hunger, and drink grind the family down step by step.
lost-in-the-air:
Lost in the Air is a boys' adventure novel by Roy J. Snell, issued in 1920. It belongs to his Mystery Stories for Boys. The heroes, Bruce Manning and Barney Menter, are young fliers fresh from army air service. They now work in the wilds of northern Canada, near Hudson Bay.

Their flight north brings a strange landing, a walrus hunt, and a battle under the Arctic moon. Chapters promise a treasure city, a mystery cavern, and a wreck. The boys fight criminals and brave the ice to reach the Pole itself. Snell fills the tale with planes, snow, and quick action. It is fast, old-fashioned adventure for young readers.
lothair:
Lothair is a novel by Benjamin Disraeli, the Earl of Beaconsfield. Its hero, Lothair, is a young and wealthy English nobleman. Great forces compete for his soul as he enters the world. The Roman Catholic Church courts him through a charming cardinal and priests.

Secret revolutionary societies also claim him, through the brave Theodora. English country-house society offers him a third, safer path. Disraeli, himself a prime minister, knew this world of power and faith well. The novel mixes romance with sharp talk on religion and politics. It was one of the most debated English novels of its day.
nasa-tm-19700007983-evaluation-with-a-tu:
Willis M. Braithwaite, John H. Dicus, and John E. Moss Jr. ran this study at the Lewis Research Center. Their report came out in January 1970. They used a turbofan engine to test air jets as a way to distort the air flow at the engine inlet.

Engineers need uneven inlet flow to test how an engine behaves in real flight. The team compared air jets with the screens then in common use. Both ways had to make the same half-circle pattern of distorted flow. The results are given as engine stall limits and inlet flow profiles, and the two systems made much the same profiles.
nasa-tm-19700028160-titanium-8al-1mo-1v-:
Ronald L. Nichols of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory wrote this report on September 12, 1969. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. It covers the repair of a crossbeam made of titanium alloy 8Al-1Mo-1V, a structural part whose cracks had to be understood before they could be fixed.

The report opens with the part's history, then moves through testing and a close crack analysis. Photographs show weld seams carrying tungsten left by the electrode, pores with trailing tails, and brittle fracture surfaces under the microscope. The repair section then gives the working steps in order: machining and cleaning first, then welding. Conclusions state what the shop learned from the job.
our-pilots-in-the-air:
Captain William B. Perry's Our Pilots in the Air is a boys' war novel of the First World War's air war in eastern France. Chapter one, A Bombing Air Raid, opens on a Flying Camp in eastern France. Hangars and queer-shaped buildings spread over trampled green. A placard on the bulletin board puts Bombing Squadron members on the alert at seven that evening.

Two young aviators read the notice together: Orry and his smaller, dark-eyed companion. They tease each other about shaking hands on the crank. Their last dive away from a Fokker nearly ended them, until a Tommy in a monoplane helped. Perry writes the new air service as adventure for the boys who were already dreaming of cockpits.
outlaws-of-the-air: George Chetwynd Griffith's Outlaws of the Air is an early novel of aerial warfare. This edition is dated 1897. Griffith pioneered the future-war story in English. The hosted sample shows a contents list only. Its forty-one titles sketch the whole machine. A utopia in the south and the Red Pirate appear. So do the Destroyer at work and the War-Hawk's first flight. No chapter text appears.
