poems-of-henry-timrod-with-memoir:
Henry Timrod, the South Carolina poet who became the laureate of the Confederacy, is presented here in a collected Poems with a memoir of his life. An introduction by the late Judge George S. Bryan frames the work. Timrod wrote lyrics of spring, love, and southern landscape before the Civil War consumed his health and his world. He died young, leaving a small body of intensely finished verse.

Contents include Spring, the Cotton Boll, his famous ode on the crop that ruled the South. Courtship poems and serenades, and pieces such as the Arctic Voyager and a Vision of Poesy. Later pages turn to 1866 and the wreckage after defeat. The memoir matters as much as the poems: Timrod's reputation was built posthumously by southern readers who saw their own lost world in his lines. This volume is the shrine they built him.
proserpina-volume-2-studies-of-wayside-f:
John Ruskin continued his studies of wayside flowers in a second volume dated 1888, subtitled with a memory of pure air in the Alps and in his father's Scotland and England. Ruskin planned a new ordering of plants based on close looking.

The volume opens with the violet, whose group he calls the Cytherides, and explains why its placing needs care. Ruskin warns readers not to expect pretty writing, saying that time is past for him. What they get instead is fierce, exact attention to leaf and flower, mixed with grief at a spoiled world.
red-hair:
Elinor Glyn copyrighted this novel in 1905, when it first appeared as The Vicissitudes of Evangeline; the Authors' Press later reissued it as Red Hair. Its heroine writes her own story, starting at Branches Park on November 3. She wonders if it is amusing to be an adventuress, since that is what she expects to become.

She has beauty, skill with hair and hats, and only three hundred pounds a year to live on. Mrs. Carruthers, who raised her, meant to leave her a fortune but made no proper will. The heir takes all, and the girl she detested yet kept is left with nothing but her looks and wit.
samantha-at-the-world-s-fair:
Josiah Allen's Wife, Marietta Holley, wrote Samantha at the World's Fair, illustrated by Baron C. de Grimm and issued at New York in 1893 by Funk and Wagnalls. The book is given to Columbia, who has just sailed out and discovered woman, and to the sect discovered. A front picture shows Samantha and Josiah overwhelmed, the minute they passed the gate, by the unspeakable aspect of the buildings. Copyright was taken in 1893 and the work registered at Stationer's Hall in London.

The preface opens on a beautiful evening in Jonesville, and in the world. The earth sat peaceful and serene under the glowing light of a full moon and some stars. Samantha sat just as peaceful and calm under the mellow light of their hanging lamp. Beside her shone what she calls the blue radiance of her companion's two orbs, meaning Josiah's eyes.
that-mainwaring-affair:
Maynard Barbour wrote That Mainwaring Affair, a mystery novel in twenty-seven chapters. Chapter heads point to a will, an inquest, and a court fight. Titles include The Last Will and Testament of Hugh Mainwaring. The Weaving of the Web and The Silent Witness also stand out.

Chapter one opens on a hot July day. The scene is the plush private offices of Mainwaring and Co., stock brokers. Sun forces thin shafts of light through tight shutters. The light gilds the dim, rich rooms. From that firm base the tale spins out a death. A lost or forged will comes next. Kin then war over a vast estate. Readers get a brisk period mystery of greed, hidden pasts, and proof found at the last hour.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-the-county-fair: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at the County Fair, put out in New York by Grosset and Dunlap with rights dated 1922. A note on the title page says the book was made in war time under state rules to save paper, yet is whole and not cut down. Its first parts are The Broken Bridge, a cry of There's a Snake, The Merry-Go-Round, and A Missing Coat. Sam Is Worried and Happy Days Coming close the part names shown. A plate shows Freddie in a race.
the-book-of-noodles-stories-of-simpleton:
W. A. Clouston wrote The Book of Noodles: Stories of Simpletons; or, Fools and Their Follies, put out in London by Elliot Stock in 1888. Clouston had also written on how folk tales move and change from land to land. He gave the book to his friend David Ross of Glasgow. A line from Twelfth Night stands at the front: this is the best fooling when all is done.

In his preface Clouston says tales of fools, like folk tales at large, have no clear first source. Greek jests of this kind, he thinks, had drifted among many peoples long before they were set in type. The first such tales that can be dated come from old Buddhist books, most of all the Jatakas, or Birth-stories. Those tales were said to have been told by Gautama to his flock, and many deal with silly folk and dull beasts.
the-dialect-of-the-west-of-england-parti: James Jennings, secretary of the Metropolitan Literary Institution, compiled The Dialect of the West of England, particularly Somersetshire. It holds a glossary of words in use there, and pieces showing the dialect. The title page states that the work rests on the second edition. The whole was revised, corrected, and enlarged by James Knight Jennings, M.A., a scholar and librarian. Two dissertations on the Anglo-Saxon pronouns are added. A verse in dialect, from a piece called The Farewell, stands first. Only the front matter is present here.
the-elixir:
Georg Ebers's tale The Elixir opens in Leipzig, in a tall gabled house on Katherinenstrasse long held by his kin. The house, once called The Three Kings, bore the sign of the court apothecary, its three patron saints bright with paint and gold. Ebers says much worth saving happened there, and he means to chronicle his forebear's strange life as his grandmother told it.

That forebear sought a drug to stretch life, and the hunt bent his days. Ebers, an Egyptologist turned novelist, sets the tale in old Leipzig with love for its streets and craft lore.
the-faery-tales-of-weir:
Anna McClure Sholl wrote The Faery Tales of Weir, printed in 1908. Six tales make up the book. They tell of a blue glove and of a golden archer. Other tales bring an invisible wall, a tree in a dark wood, a cat that winked, and magic tears.

The opening paints Weir as a hushed town where real faery tales are still told in shadowy nurseries. Shops have dim, stained windows, houses sleep under thick trees, and small churches ring with hoarse, sweet bells. Into that drowsy, charmed town the tales bring magic objects, hidden walls, and gifts that test the hearts of those who find them.
the-felon-s-track-or-history-of-the-atte:
Michael Doheny wrote The Felon's Track, a history of the failed rising in Ireland that covers the years 1843 to the close of 1848. This Dublin printing of 1920 adds D'Arcy M'Gee's own tale of 1848.

Doheny took part in the Young Ireland movement and fled when the rising fell apart. His book traces the path from open agitation to armed revolt and defeat. A preface, notes on the author's fellows, and an index round out the volume. The title's felon is the hunted rebel, and the track is the road to exile that many such men walked.
the-hosts-of-the-air: Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Hosts of the Air, subtitled the story of a quest in the Great War, with pictures by Charles Wrenn, published in New York and London by D. Appleton and Company in 1915. Altsheler is named as the author of The Guns of Europe and The Forest of Swords. The pages present add lists for his Civil War series and World War series, naming The Star of Gettysburg and The Guns of Bull Run. Only the title pages and series lists are present here.
the-mastery-of-the-air:
William J. Claxton's The Mastery of the Air deals mainly with real achievements by the pioneers of flight. Claxton states in his preface that the book makes no pretence of going minutely into technical science. His chief object is to wake an intelligent interest in flying among ordinary readers. The Great War, he notes, gave a tremendous impetus to the contest for mastery of the air.

The opening part treats balloons and airships, starting with man's duel with nature. A chapter credits a French paper-maker with inventing the balloon. Claxton thanks the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service for illustrations and information. Aviation firms such as Sopwith and A. V. Roe also helped him. Readers get the romance of early flight and wartime flying, written for the general public rather than the expert.
the-oakdale-affair:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The Oakdale Affair, a tale that opens at night outside a banker's house. A young prowler watches the house of Jonas Prim, president of the First National Bank of Oakdale, and notes that the family is at dinner and the upper floor is empty. The youth has already stolen a suit and cap from the chauffeur's rooms above the garage.

Burroughs stresses that the intruder is no hardened thief. The boy's strained face and slender build suggest a beginner steeling himself for a crime. He crosses the lawn boldly, passes the open hall door on purpose, and seems to know the house and its habits well.
the-open-air: Richard Jefferies gathered his nature papers under the title The Open Air. In a short note he thanks the editors of The Standard, Longman's Magazine, the Manchester Guardian, and other papers where the pieces first appeared. That note and a contents list are the whole of what is present; the essays themselves are absent. The contents list Saint Guido, Wild Flowers, Sunny Brighton, The Pine Wood, Nature on the Roof, The Modern Thames, The Haunt of the Hare, Downs, and Forest.
the-philosophy-of-despair:
David Starr Jordan wrote The Philosophy of Despair, dedicated to John Maxson Stillman in token of good cheer. A poem at the front imagines his epitaph on a stone by the sea: jungle and town and reef and sea, I loved God's earth and his earth loved me. The essay then declares that today is the only day we have, the day in which we play our part.

Our part, Jordan says, is action, not whining, and love, not cynicism, expressed as human helpfulness. Any other course leads toward decay and waste. He takes his text from FitzGerald's version of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, quoting the angel of the darker drink. Despair, in his handling, becomes a call to work.
the-poetical-works-of-henry-kirk-white-w: The Poetical Works of Henry Kirke White comes with a memoir by Sir Harris Nicolas. Here only the title page, dedication, and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. After the memoir, miscellaneous poems are listed: Clifton Grove, Time, and Childhood in two parts. The Christiad appears too. Other entries include lines on a survey of the heavens, a summer's eve description, and verses in the prospect of death. Nelsoni Mors appears, plus an elegy for Mr. Gill, drowned in the Trent while bathing.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol:
The Iron Gate and Other Poems (1877 to 1881) form this section of Holmes's Poetical Works, bracketed as Volume 3 of the 1893 set. The contents list verses for Whittier's seventieth birthday and the Moore centennial. The American Academy centennial appears, and the Massachusetts Medical Society's centennial dinner. The School-Boy and The Silent Melody appear too.

The opening poem, The Iron Gate, was read at the breakfast given in honour of Holmes's seventieth birthday by the publishers of the Atlantic Monthly at Boston on December 3, 1879. It begins by asking where this patriarch is whom the company is kindly greeting. The name is not unfamiliar, the poem says. Nor is it unknown to many a joyous meeting in days long vanished. The question hanging over the verse is whether he is still the same, or changed by years, forgotten and forgetting.
the-poetical-works-of-william-lisle-bowl: Volume I of The Poetical Works of William Lisle Bowles was edited by the Reverend George Gilfillan, with memoir and explanatory notes. James Nichol published it at Edinburgh in 1855. Bowles is styled canon of St. Paul's Cathedral and rector of Bremhill. Here only the title pages and the start of the contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The contents open with sonnets at Tynemouth Priory after a tempestuous voyage and at Bamborough Castle. Others stand on the Wainsbeck, Tweed, and Itchin, and one marks resigning an Oxford scholarship.
the-war-in-the-air:
H. G. Wells wrote The War in the Air in 1907, and a preface to the reprint edition, signed K., asks readers to grasp that date firmly. The novel appeared as a serial in 1908 and in book form that fall. Aeroplanes were then a rumour for most people, and the sausage balloon held the air.

The preface concedes weak spots: few anti-aircraft guns and still less thought of submarines. Yet Prince Karl, a fantasy in 1908, has since been copied faithfully by reality, the preface claims. Wells's warning stands: continued war means civilisation's smash-up, leaving a choice between chaos and a united world. Contents chapters send Bert Smallways from a balloon into a German air-fleet, a battle over the North Atlantic, and war coming to New York.
